### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Perry et al. (2026) is a large (N = 5,550), single-wave, single-informant survey study drawn from the 2020–21 APA Task Force on Violence Against Educators, and the field should read it as a well-powered correlational description rather than as the mechanism-and-moderation study its title and abstract announce. What it establishes is narrow but solid: teachers who report more support from their principal report substantially lower intent to transfer (β ≈ −.36) and to quit (β ≈ −.23), they report feeling safer and less anxious, and teachers reporting more student-perpetrated victimization are worse off on every measure. These associations are precisely estimated, essentially unchanged across the paper's two model specifications, and — unusually — fully reproducible from the Table 1 correlation matrix, which this review verified independently (the reproduction also shows that the demographic and school covariates move the estimates by about .01, so the published coefficients are the bivariate correlations, decomposed). What the paper does not establish is the claim it is named for. 'Necessary' is untestable in this design. 'Not sufficient' rests on two p = .02 interactions among eight tests with no multiplicity adjustment, none of which is significant for transfer intentions, in a moderation model whose 'standardized' victimization main effects (−1.69 and −1.74, sign-reversed from the raw correlations of +.36 and −.36) signal uncentered product terms on an uninterpretable metric, and whose own Figure 2 shows the support–quit slope barely moving (roughly −.33 to −.31) across the plotted range of victimization. Around that sit a mediation model called 'good fit' at RMSEA .08 and CFI .91 against the paper's own stated cutoffs of <.05 and >.95, a Results sentence that inverts the sign of the paper's largest mediator path, a Discussion summary contradicted by Table 3 and by the paper's own later paragraph, a 'latent constructs' novelty claim contradicted by the composite-score analysis, an opening teacher-attrition statistic cited to a report on principals, no data or code statement, and no account of what the paper adds beyond the same team's several prior papers on the same survey. The paper is therefore useful with caveats, at the lower edge of that category: cite it, from its tables, for the size and consistency of the support–retention-intention association and for how little of that association runs through safety and anxiety/stress; treat the moderation and the title as a hypothesis the study raised rather than one it tested; and count it as one specification from a shared 2020–21 dataset, not as independent corroboration of its sibling papers.

#### Key Strengths

- A large, precisely estimated national teacher sample (N = 5,550) recruited with a priori stratification, analyzed with appropriate robust (MLR) estimation, a reported measurement model, pre-stated fit criteria, and a documented clustering check (state-level ICCs of .006–.018).
- The core associations are robust and independently verifiable: every Table 2 coefficient and all four indirect effects reproduce from the Table 1 correlation matrix to within rounding, and the direct paths are essentially unchanged between the mediation model (Table 2) and the moderation model (Table 3).
- A real conceptual increment over the team's prior papers on the same survey: administrator support promoted to focal predictor, and student victimization treated as a moderating context rather than a predictor or outcome — the paper's most portable idea, offered as an agenda for the field.
- An underplayed but useful negative result: the indirect effects through safety and anxiety/stress (−.03 to −.05) are an order of magnitude smaller than the direct effects (−.23 to −.36), so roughly four-fifths of the support–intention association does not run through these well-being channels — evidence against well-being-only accounts of why supportive principals retain teachers.
- A candid Limitations section that concedes cross-sectionality, self-report, intentions rather than turnover (citing Nguyen et al., 2025), unmodeled school- and district-level clustering, and the possibility that victimization drove differential survey response — nearly a complete account of why the estimates should be read as descriptive associations.

#### Key Concerns

- The title claim is not established. 'Necessary' cannot be tested by a correlational main effect, and 'not sufficient' rests on Support × Victimization and Anxiety × Victimization interactions on quit intentions at p = .02 (β = ±.12), with all three transfer-intention interactions null (p = .64, .38, .11) and Figure 2c showing the support–quit slope moving only from about −.33 to −.31 across the plotted range of victimization.
- The moderation model — the source of the paper's novel finding — is on an uninterpretable metric as printed and cannot be checked: victimization 'standardized' main effects of −1.69 and −1.74 (sign-reversed from Table 1's r = +.36 and −.36) are the signature of uncentered product terms with STDYX standardization applied to interactions; Figure 2's plotted slopes cannot be reconciled with Table 3's coefficients; Figure 1 silently merges the two models (and prints .39 where Table 3 says 0.40); and no unstandardized estimates, syntax, or centering description is provided.
- The prose repeatedly disagrees with the exhibits, so the narrative cannot be quoted without checking the tables: the mediation model is called 'good fit' at RMSEA .08 / CFI .91 against stated cutoffs of <.05 / >.95; the Results say anxiety/stress 'was negatively related to quit intentions' when Table 2 reports +0.25 (and invent an anxiety→safety path); the Discussion summary claims moderation of 'transfer and quit intentions' that Table 3 refutes and the paper's own later parenthetical ('but not transfer') corrects; 'teachers with higher rates of victimization were very likely to quit teaching' describes an intentions scale on which victimization's main effect is β = .12, p = .19; and the abstract uses 'the effect of administrative support.'
- Design limits inherited by every estimate: cross-sectional and single-informant with no common-method check; an opt-in vendor-list and union/social-media sample with no response rate or weights; outcome scales in which one of three items is a COVID-19 attribution; a 'causal order' claim resting on retrospective item wording while the administrator-support scale has no reference period at all; a discipline item in the support scale that overlaps mechanically with the victimization moderator; covariates that provide no adjustment; and missing-data handling that is never stated despite documented item nonresponse and a constant N = 5,550.
- Positioning and transparency gaps: the 'one of the first to utilize multi-item latent constructs' novelty claim is contradicted by the composite-score path analysis and the dichotomized victimization count; the opening teacher quit/transfer statistics are cited to the NCES Principal Follow-Up Survey report; the paper never delineates its increment over McMahon, Swenski et al. (2024), McMahon, Worrell et al. (2024), Reddy et al. (2024), and Astor et al. (2024) on the same survey; the education-policy and economics literature on principals and teacher retention is essentially absent (Boyd et al. 2011 cited only definitionally; Ladd, Grissom, Kraft, Papay missing); and there is no data availability statement, no code, and an unreported sensitivity analysis.

#### What to Rely On

- Perceived administrator support is among the strongest teacher-reported correlates of intent to transfer (β ≈ −.36) and to quit (β ≈ −.23) in a large 2020–21 U.S. teacher sample — verified from Table 1's correlation matrix; take the numbers from Table 2, not from the text.
- Teachers who report more administrator support report less anxiety/stress (β ≈ −.19) and more safety (β ≈ .28), and both of those in turn track lower intent to leave (anxiety→quit ≈ +.25, safety→transfer ≈ −.17) — as directions and rough magnitudes of cross-sectional associations.
- The mediated share is small: indirect effects of −.03 to −.05 against direct effects of −.23 to −.36, so roughly 75–85% of the support–intention association does not run through perceived safety or anxiety/stress. This is the paper's most useful and least advertised quantitative result.
- Teachers reporting more student-perpetrated victimization report lower safety, higher anxiety/stress, and higher transfer and quit intentions (zero-order correlations of .25 to .36 in absolute value) — as descriptive correlations from Table 1, not as the coefficients in Table 3.
- The framing proposal that teacher victimization is better modeled as a moderating context than as a predictor or outcome — as an agenda-setting idea and a demonstration that the analysis is feasible at scale, not as settled evidence about the size of that moderation.
- The paper's map of the violence-against-educators literature (Longobardi et al. 2019; Berkowitz et al. 2022; McMahon et al. 2017; Reddy et al. 2018; NCES crime-and-safety indicators) is current and usable as an entry point to that subfield.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- 'Necessary but Not Sufficient' and 'administrator support did little to buffer this' — necessity is untestable here, the retention-outcome interactions are p = .02 among eight uncorrected tests and null for transfer, and Figure 2c shows the support–quit association essentially undiminished at high victimization.
- Every coefficient in Table 3, including the interaction terms (+0.40, −0.42, ±0.12) — the victimization main effects of −1.69 and −1.74 (sign-reversed from r = +.36 and −.36) indicate uncentered product terms on a non-interpretable standardized metric; Figure 2 and Table 3 do not reconcile; request unstandardized estimates before citing any magnitude.
- The abstract's and Discussion summary's claim that victimization weakened the relation between support and 'retention intentions' or 'transfer and quit intentions' — all three transfer-intention interactions are null; the paper's own later parenthetical, 'but not transfer,' is the accurate version.
- The 'unexpected' finding that victimization weakens the anxiety→quit link — β = −.12 at p = .02, opposite to Hypothesis 3, a slope difference of about .04 in Figure 2d, and a post hoc explanation that reverses the modeled path's direction.
- Causal language throughout ('the effect of administrative support,' 'influence,' 'establishing causal order') — the design is cross-sectional and single-informant, the administrator-support items carry no reference period, and the Limitations section retracts the causal-order claim.
- 'Teachers with higher rates of victimization were very likely to quit teaching' — the outcome is a five-point intentions scale, one-third of which is a COVID-19 attribution item, and Table 3's victimization main effect on quit intentions is β = .12, p = .19.
- The mediation as evidence of mechanism, and the exact indirect-effect magnitudes — the mediation model fails the paper's own fit cutoffs (RMSEA .08, CFI .91), composites leave measurement error uncorrected, and mediator–outcome confounding (e.g., negative affectivity) is unaddressed; read it as a descriptive decomposition of a correlation matrix.
- The Results sentence 'anxiety/stress was positively related to safety perceptions and was negatively related to quit intentions (see Table 2)' — both clauses invert the paper's own numbers (r = −.32; β = +.25); do not quote it.
- 'National sample' and any prevalence-style figure — recruitment was an opt-in commercial email list plus union and association distribution including social media, with no response rate, no denominator, and no weights; the demographic match to NCES does not address selection on victimization or intent to leave.
- Transporting the estimates beyond 2020–21 — one of three items in each outcome scale names COVID-19, and the mediators are mid-pandemic recollections of pre-pandemic conditions.
- 'One of the first to utilize multi-item latent constructs' and the 'structural equation modeling' keyword — the structural model is path analysis on composite scores, and victimization is a count of dichotomized items; do not cite this paper for a latent-variable measurement advance.
- The opening quit/transfer statistics attributed to Taie & Lewis (2023) — the listed reference is the NCES Principal Follow-Up Survey report; verify against the Teacher Follow-Up Survey report, and note those are one-year rates.
- Counting this paper as independent evidence alongside McMahon, Swenski et al. (2024), McMahon, Worrell et al. (2024), Reddy et al. (2024), Astor et al. (2024), and Peist et al. (2024) — these draw on the same or adjacent 2020–21 data; map the overlap before pooling effect sizes.
- The Implications section's recommendations (administrator professional development, MTSS-framed supports, discipline-policy reform, peer mentoring) — nothing in the study measures any intervention; treat these as informed opinion, not conclusions licensed by the analyses.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

A large (N = 5,550), competently executed path analysis on a non-probability national teacher survey, whose descriptive core — administrator support is negatively associated with transfer and quit intentions, partly through perceived safety and anxiety/stress — is stable across specifications and reproduces the raw correlation matrix almost exactly. But the design is cross-sectional and single-informant, the paper's claim to have 'established causal order' via retrospective item wording does not survive scrutiny, the primary mediation model fails the paper's own stated fit criteria (RMSEA .08, CFI .91 against thresholds of <.05 and >.95), Table 3's victimization coefficients are on an uninterpretable metric (β = −1.69 on anxiety, opposite in sign to the r = +.36 in Table 1), and the moderation results that carry the title's 'not sufficient' claim rest on two p = .02 coefficients out of eight interaction tests whose own Figure 2 shows a substantively negligible effect. Read the associations; do not read the mechanism or the buffering story.

**Strengths:**

- Large sample (N = 5,550) with recruitment stratified a priori on region, school level, role, and urbanicity, yielding precise estimates (SEs of .01–.02) and a demographic profile the authors benchmark against NCES teacher statistics.
- Estimation choices are appropriate for the data type: MLR (robust ML) throughout to handle non-normality, a confirmatory measurement model estimated and reported before the structural analyses (RMSEA .04, CFI .95, SRMR .04), and explicit a priori fit criteria stated in the Measures section.
- The core structural paths are genuinely robust: every direct path is essentially unchanged between the mediation model (Table 2) and the moderation model (Table 3) — support→anxiety −.19/−.19, support→safety .28/.23, support→transfer −.36/−.35, support→quit −.23/−.26, anxiety→quit .25/.25. Findings that replicate across two specifications with different covariance structures are not artifacts of one model.
- Clustering was checked rather than assumed: a null model produced state-level ICCs of .006–.018, and the authors are candid that school/district clustering could not be assessed because most schools contributed only one or two respondents (which, notably, also means design effects at that level are likely small).
- The dichotomization of the 11 victimization items was subjected to a sensitivity analysis using the original mean-composite scale (footnote 1), with results reported as unchanged.
- The Limitations section is unusually honest for this literature: it explicitly states the data are 'methodologically cross-sectional, limiting our ability to determine the temporal order among variables or make causal inferences,' names retrospective recall bias, names intention-vs-turnover slippage, and raises the possibility that victimization itself drove differential survey response.

**Weaknesses:**

- No response rate, no sampling denominator, and no weights. Recruitment combined a purchased commercial list (MCH Strategic Data, built from web scrapes of public sources) with open link distribution by NEA, AFT, NASP, and SSWAA 'through varied methods, such as email or social media.' The social-media arm makes the denominator unknowable in principle. The only calibration offered is that demographics are 'comparable to national statistics' — but demographic comparability says nothing about selection on the study's actual variables (victimization exposure, job dissatisfaction, intent to leave), which is exactly the selection the authors themselves flag in Limitation 5.
- The 'establishing causal order' claim in the Measures section is manufactured by item wording, not by design, and it is contradicted by the paper's own Limitations section. Safety and anxiety/stress reference the 2019–20 pre-COVID period; victimization references August 2019–March 2020; outcomes reference survey time. But administrator support — the independent variable, the first link in the entire chain — is given no reference period at all in the Measures section. If teachers answered about their current principal (the natural reading, and what Procedures implies), the presumed ordering fails at step one.
- The outcome scales are not clean measures of retention intent: one of the three transfer items and one of the three quit items is 'COVID-19 has increased my desire to transfer/quit.' One-third of each outcome composite is a pandemic-attribution item, which both anchors the outcome to a post-COVID appraisal (undercutting the retrospective ordering) and limits generalization of the outcome construct beyond 2020–21.
- The primary mediation model — the model producing every number in Table 2, including all four indirect effects — is described as having 'good fit to the data' at RMSEA = .08 [.08, .09], CFI = .91, SRMR = .02. This fails the paper's own pre-registered-in-text thresholds (RMSEA < .05, CFI > .95). The escape clause the authors wrote for themselves ('elevated RMSEA values were considered indicative of acceptable model fit when occurring with values in acceptable ranges for all other indices') does not apply, because CFI is also out of range; only SRMR passes, and SRMR is the index least sensitive to omitted structural paths.
- Path analysis on composite scores, despite the paper's central novelty claim to use 'multi-item latent constructs.' The Data Analysis section states plainly that 'structural relationships between constructs in our analytical model were assessed with composite scores.' Measurement error is therefore uncorrected, and its known consequence in mediation is directional: unreliability in the mediators attenuates the indirect effects and inflates the direct effect — precisely the decomposition the 'necessary but not sufficient' argument depends on.
- Table 3's victimization main effects are not interpretable as reported. β = −1.69 on anxiety/stress and β = −1.74 on safety, in a table labeled standardized (Figure 1 note: 'All coefficients are standardized estimates'). The anxiety coefficient is opposite in sign to the Table 1 correlation of +.36, and both are roughly five times the magnitude of any bivariate association in the paper. In a product-term model these are conditional slopes at the other variable's zero point; administrator support is on a 1–5 scale with M = 4.05, so a slope evaluated at support = 0 is an extrapolation off the end of the response scale. Centering is never mentioned, and Mplus STDYX standardization of product terms and their conditional main effects is a known trap. The paper never remarks on the sign reversal, and Figure 1 omits these paths entirely, so a reader working from the figure never encounters the anomaly.
- Eight interaction coefficients were tested across four outcome equations with no multiplicity adjustment. Four were significant, but the two that carry the paper's headline retention claim are at p = .02 (Support × Victimization on quit, β = .12, CI [.02, .22]; Anxiety × Victimization on quit, β = −.12, CI [−.22, −.02]). Neither survives even a lenient correction (Bonferroni across the six outcome-equation interactions gives α = .008). All three interactions on transfer intentions are null (p = .64, .38, .11).
- Figure 2 undercuts the paper's own rhetoric. Panel 2c plots the administrator support → quit intentions simple slope across ±1 SD of victimization: it moves from roughly −.33 to −.31, a change of about .02 standardized units, with wide overlapping confidence bands. Panel 2d shows the anxiety → quit slope moving from about .38 to .34. These are the two effects behind 'administrator support did little to buffer this' and the title's 'Not Sufficient.' The support–quit association remains strongly negative at high victimization. (Panels 2a and 2b, the p < .001 interactions on anxiety and safety, are more substantial — slopes of −.19 → −.13 and .22 → .17 — but those are not the retention outcomes the title is about.)
- No missing-data section anywhere. N = 5,550 is reported in every table note, yet the Participants section documents item-level missingness on variables used as covariates in every model: 34 missing gender, 69 missing race/ethnicity, 110 missing school level, 24 missing urbanicity. Mplus conditions on exogenous covariates rather than modeling them, so unless the authors did something they never describe, the analytic N is below 5,550. Free/reduced-price-lunch percentage is also a covariate and its missingness is never mentioned at all. The estimation sample cannot be reconstructed.
- Every construct in the model — predictor, both mediators, both outcomes, and the moderator — comes from the same teacher, on the same instrument, in the same sitting. There is no marker variable, no Harman-type test, no method factor, and no external validation against records. The measurement model demonstrates that items load on their intended factors; it does not rule out a common evaluative factor inflating every structural path. The Limitations section names self-report and social desirability but does not connect this to inflation of the structural estimates.
- Mediator–outcome confounding is unaddressed. The covariate set is demographics plus four school characteristics; it contains nothing on workload, salary, class size, school behavioral climate, personal mental-health history, or family circumstances. Negative affectivity alone would confound anxiety→quit. Notably, the covariates do almost no work: total effects reconstructed from Table 2 (transfer: −.36 − .03 − .05 = −.44; quit: −.23 − .05 − .03 = −.31) match the raw Table 1 correlations of −.45 and −.31 to within .01, so these are not meaningfully 'adjusted' estimates.
- Construct overlap between the predictor and the moderator. One of three administrator-support items is 'My head of school or principal supports me in matters of discipline.' Teachers experiencing more student aggression have a mechanical reason to rate that item lower, so the Support × Victimization term is partly an interaction of victimization with itself. The authors raise the discipline item in the Discussion as a substantive point but never as a threat to the moderation analysis.
- A printed Results sentence contradicts its own table. Line-level: 'In turn, anxiety/stress was positively related to safety perceptions and was negatively related to quit intentions (see Table 2).' Table 2 reports anxiety → quit intentions at β = +0.25, p < .001, and Table 1 gives the anxiety–safety correlation as −.32. Both halves of the sentence are wrong in direction.
- No R² or variance-explained statistic is reported for any endogenous variable, and covariate coefficients are suppressed everywhere ('Nonsignificant and covariate estimates are not presented for clarity'), so readers cannot judge how much of the outcome variance the model accounts for or whether any control does meaningful work.
- Indirect-effect confidence intervals appear to be delta-method/symmetric (e.g., −.05 with CI [−.06, −.04]) rather than bootstrapped, which is not standard practice for products of coefficients — though at N = 5,550 this is a minor concern relative to the others.
- The moderation model (RMSEA .05, CFI .93) fits better than the mediation model, yet the authors state that 'main effects were not interpreted in this second iteration.' The better-fitting model's structural coefficients are set aside in favor of the worse-fitting model's — an odd inversion, mitigated only by the fact that the two sets of estimates turn out to be nearly identical.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely on the direct associations, not on the causal or mechanistic language surrounding them. 'Teachers who report more administrator support also report substantially lower intent to transfer (β ≈ −.36) and quit (β ≈ −.23)' is well-supported and replicates across two model specifications. 'Administrator support reduces turnover intent' is not what these data show, and the paper's own Limitations section agrees.
- Discount all effect magnitudes for common-method variance before citing them. Predictor, mediators, moderator, and outcomes are one teacher's answers on one questionnaire at one moment. Treat the reported βs as upper bounds on any real association, and note that the total effects reproduce the raw bivariate correlations almost exactly — the demographic and school controls move the association by about .01, so these are not usefully 'adjusted' estimates.
- Treat the mediation results as a descriptive decomposition of a correlation matrix, not as evidence about mechanism. Read the indirect effects for their size, which is small: mediation through safety and anxiety accounts for about .08 of the −.44 total effect on transfer intent (roughly 18%) and about .08 of the −.31 total on quit intent (roughly 26%). The dominant path is the unmediated one — which is also the path most exposed to a single underlying 'how bad is my job' appraisal.
- Do not cite Table 3's victimization main effects. β = −1.69 on anxiety is opposite in sign to the paper's own Table 1 correlation of +.36 and is not on an interpretable standardized metric. It is a conditional slope at administrator support = 0, off the end of a 1–5 scale, in a model where centering is never described. Whatever the underlying association between victimization and teacher anxiety is, this number is not an estimate of it — Table 1's r = +.36 is the more trustworthy summary.
- Read the moderation claim through Figure 2, not through the abstract or the title. The abstract's 'higher rates of victimization weakened the relationship between administrator support and retention intentions' is true only for quit intentions (all three transfer interactions are null, p = .64/.38/.11), rests on p = .02 among eight untested-for-multiplicity interactions, and Figure 2c shows the support→quit slope moving only from roughly −.33 to −.31 across ±1 SD of victimization. Support looks about as protective at high victimization as at low. The 'Not Sufficient' half of the title is a directional hint, not an established finding.
- Ignore the 'unexpected' finding that victimization weakens the anxiety→quit link (β = −.12, p = .02). It contradicts the paper's own Hypothesis 3, is one of two marginal results among eight tests, has a slope difference in Figure 2d of about .04, and the post hoc explanation offered (that certainty of leaving reduces anxiety) reverses the direction of the modeled path and is untestable in cross-sectional data.
- Note that the primary mediation model does not meet the fit standards the paper itself set two pages earlier (RMSEA .08 vs. <.05; CFI .91 vs. >.95). Misfit of that size in a path model on composites usually signals an omitted structural path or an unmodeled residual covariance — the anxiety–safety residual covariance (their bivariate r is −.32) is the obvious candidate, and if omitted it would bias exactly the two indirect effects the paper reports. Before building on the specific indirect-effect magnitudes, treat them as provisional.
- Treat the sample as a large opt-in convenience sample of teachers, not a national probability sample. There is no response rate, part of the recruitment ran through union social media, and the authors themselves note that victimization experience could plausibly drive who responded in either direction. Prevalence-style claims (how common victimization is, how many teachers intend to leave) should not be taken from this sample; the associations are the usable output.
- Do not generalize the outcome construct beyond the pandemic period without care. One of three items in each retention scale explicitly asks about COVID-19's effect on the desire to leave, and the mediators are retrospective recollections of pre-COVID conditions gathered mid-pandemic. Whether these associations hold in a normal school year is untested here.
- Verify the analytic N before using this paper as a benchmark. N = 5,550 appears in every table note, but the Participants section reports missingness on four covariates used in every model, no missing-data method is described anywhere, and free/reduced-price-lunch coverage is never discussed. The true estimation sample is probably somewhat smaller.
- Read this paper as a well-powered correlational description of one moment in U.S. teaching, whose value lies in the size and consistency of the support–retention association and in its concurrent measurement of victimization — not as evidence about what administrators can or cannot accomplish. Pair it with designs that can actually identify the effect (within-teacher panels, principal turnover as a shock, administrative turnover records) before drawing any policy conclusion about administrator training as a retention lever.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**What the design can and cannot do.** This is a single-wave, single-informant online survey of 5,550 pre-K–12 teachers fielded August 2020–June 2021, analyzed as a path model in Mplus 8.8 with MLR. Every quantity in the model — administrator support, perceived safety, anxiety/stress, victimization, and transfer and quit intentions — is one teacher's self-report on one instrument at one sitting. The paper attempts to purchase temporal ordering through item reference periods rather than through repeated measurement: safety and anxiety are asked about 2019–20 'prior to COVID-19 restrictions that occurred in March 2020,' victimization about August 2019 through March 2020, and the outcomes 'at the time of survey completion (August 2020–June 2021), thus establishing causal order for the primary analyses.' That sentence is the weakest claim in the paper and it is contradicted twenty pages later by the authors themselves: 'these data are methodologically cross-sectional, limiting our ability to determine the temporal order among variables or make causal inferences.' Two specific problems make the Measures-section claim untenable. First, the independent variable is given no reference period at all — the Administrator Support Scale description says only that teachers rated how they 'were supported by their school leader,' with no window, and the Procedures section says teachers were 'asked to reflect on their perceived administrator support' without specifying when. If teachers answered about their current principal, the presumed chain fails at its first link. Second, one of three transfer items and one of three quit items reads 'COVID-19 has increased my desire to transfer/quit,' which anchors a third of each outcome composite to a post-March-2020 appraisal while the mediators are mid-pandemic recollections of pre-pandemic states. Recall of one's own pre-COVID anxiety, reported while living through COVID, is colored by current affect — a mood-congruent recall channel that would inflate the mediator–outcome associations independent of any real relationship. The abstract's language, 'we examined the effect of administrative support,' should be read as loose usage rather than a defensible claim.

**Model fit.** The Measures section commits, in advance and in print, to RMSEA < .05, CFI > .95, and SRMR < .08 (Hu & Bentler, 1999), with a single stated exception: 'elevated RMSEA values were considered indicative of acceptable model fit when occurring with values in acceptable ranges for all other indices.' The measurement model clears this (RMSEA .04, CFI .95, SRMR .04). The primary mediation model does not: RMSEA = .08, 90% CI [.08, .09], CFI = .91, SRMR = .02, and it is nonetheless described as having 'good fit to the data.' The stated exception cannot rescue it, because CFI is out of range too; only SRMR passes, and SRMR is the fit index least responsive to omitted structural paths. This matters because that model — not the better-fitting moderation model — generates every number in Table 2, including all four indirect effects and therefore the entire mediation story. An RMSEA of .08 in a path model on six composites plus a covariate block means the imposed constraints are substantively violated somewhere. The most plausible candidate is an unmodeled residual covariance between the two mediators, whose observed correlation is −.32 (Table 1); omitting it would misallocate variance between the two mediated pathways and bias the reported indirect effects of −.03 and −.05 in unknown directions. The moderation model fits better (RMSEA .05, CFI .93 — CFI still short of the stated cutoff), which produces the odd situation that the authors interpret main effects only from the worse-fitting of the two models. In practice this turns out not to matter much, because the coefficients are nearly identical across the two, and that stability is the single strongest piece of reassurance in the paper.

**Composites, not latent variables.** The Study Purpose section stakes the paper's novelty on being 'one of the first to utilize multi-item latent constructs' rather than the 'unvalidated binary indicators' of prior work. The Data Analysis section then says the structural relationships 'were assessed with composite scores generated from our multi-item latent constructs.' A CFA was run to justify the composites, but the structural model is path analysis on observed means, so measurement error is uncorrected. Given alphas of .83–.90 the attenuation is not catastrophic, but its direction is exactly wrong for this paper's argument: unreliable mediators bias indirect effects downward and the direct effect upward, which is the very direct-versus-indirect contrast underwriting the framing that support operates partly through safety and anxiety and partly not. There is a second measurement move worth flagging. The 11 victimization items, originally a 0–5 frequency scale, were dichotomized to ever/never and summed (KR-20 = .79; M = 2.52, SD = 2.36). The resulting variable is a count of *types* of victimization experienced, not a rate. The paper nonetheless describes results throughout in rate language — 'as violence against educators increased,' 'teachers with higher rates of victimization.' Footnote 1 reports that re-running with a mean composite of the original scale left results unchanged, but the sensitivity results are not shown, so this cannot be checked.

**Table 3 is not on an interpretable metric.** This is the clearest execution problem in the paper. Table 3 reports the main effect of teacher victimization as β = −1.69 (SE .05) on anxiety/stress and β = −1.74 (SE .05) on safety, in a table whose companion figure declares 'All coefficients are standardized estimates.' Table 1 gives the corresponding bivariate correlations as +.36 and −.36. The anxiety coefficient is thus reversed in sign relative to the raw data and to the paper's entire theoretical framing, and both coefficients are roughly five times larger in magnitude than any other association reported anywhere in the study. The explanation is almost certainly mechanical rather than substantive: in a model containing Support × Victimization, the victimization 'main effect' is the conditional slope at administrator support = 0. Administrator support is a 1–5 frequency scale with M = 4.05, so support = 0 lies entirely off the response scale, and a conditional slope evaluated there is an extrapolation into a region with no data. Taking the anxiety coefficients at face value, the implied conditional victimization slope is −1.69 + 0.40 × support, which is near zero at the sample mean support level and never approaches +.36 anywhere in the observed range — a signal that the reported quantities are not on a common interpretable metric rather than a finding about teachers. Centering is nowhere mentioned in the Data Analysis section, which describes only using 'the define function in Mplus to generate variables representing the following interaction terms.' Compounding this, Mplus STDYX standardization applied to product terms and their accompanying conditional main effects does not yield interpretable standardized quantities, a caveat the software's own authors have long emphasized. The paper never remarks on the sign reversal, and Figure 1 does not display these paths at all — the figure note says nonsignificant and covariate estimates were omitted, but these estimates are significant at p < .001, so a reader relying on the figure never sees them. Figure 2's x-axis running from −1.1 to +1.1 suggests victimization was standardized for the simple-slope plots, which makes the retention of −1.69/−1.74 in the coefficient table harder to reconcile still.

**The moderation results and their size.** Eight interaction coefficients were estimated across four equations (one each for anxiety and safety, three each for transfer and quit). Four reached significance. Two are strong — Support × Victimization on anxiety (β = .40, p < .001) and on safety (β = −.42, p < .001) — though their magnitudes inherit the metric problems above. Two are marginal, and they are the two that carry the paper's title: Support × Victimization on quit intentions (β = .12, SE .05, p = .02, CI [.02, .22]) and Anxiety × Victimization on quit intentions (β = −.12, SE .05, p = .02, CI [−.22, −.02]). All three transfer-intention interactions are null (p = .64, .38, .11). No multiplicity adjustment is applied; a Bonferroni correction across just the six outcome-equation interactions gives α = .008, which both p = .02 results fail. But the more decisive check is the paper's own Figure 2. Panel 2c plots the administrator support → quit intentions simple slope against victimization: the fitted line runs from about −.33 at the low end to about −.31 at the high end, a shift of roughly .02 standardized units, with confidence bands spanning something like −.42 to −.22 throughout. Panel 2d shows the anxiety → quit slope moving from about .38 to .34. Against this, the Results section asserts that 'Teachers with higher rates of victimization were very likely to quit teaching, and administrator support did little to buffer this,' and the title announces 'Necessary but Not Sufficient.' The figure shows administrator support remaining strongly and negatively associated with quit intentions at every level of victimization. The 'not sufficient' conclusion is a directional hint that happened to clear p = .05, not a demonstrated attenuation. Panels 2a and 2b are more substantial in relative terms — the support→anxiety slope weakens from −.19 to −.13, and support→safety from .22 to .17 — but those concern the mediators, not retention. There is also a construct-overlap problem specific to this analysis: one of the three administrator-support items is 'My head of school or principal supports me in matters of discipline,' which teachers facing more student aggression have a direct reason to rate lower. The Support × Victimization term is therefore partly an interaction of victimization with a victimization-contaminated measure. The authors discuss this item at length in the Implications section as a substantive lever, but never as a threat to the moderation estimate.

**How much work the covariates do: none, essentially.** Reconstructing total effects from Table 2 gives −.36 − .03 − .05 = −.44 for transfer intentions and −.23 − .05 − .03 = −.31 for quit intentions. The corresponding raw correlations in Table 1 are −.45 and −.31. The full covariate block — age, gender, five race/ethnicity indicators, percent free/reduced-price lunch, three school-level indicators, and two urbanicity indicators — moves the association by about .01. Readers should therefore not treat these as adjusted estimates in any meaningful sense; they are the bivariate correlations, decomposed. Compounding this, no coefficient for any covariate is reported anywhere, and no R² is reported for any endogenous variable, so there is no way to see what the controls do or how much outcome variance the model explains.

**Missing data and the estimation sample.** There is no missing-data section. N = 5,550 appears in the note to every table, yet the Participants section itself documents item-level missingness on four variables that enter every model as covariates: 34 teachers declined gender, 69 declined race/ethnicity, 110 did not report school level, 24 did not report urbanicity. Mplus conditions on exogenous covariates rather than bringing them into the likelihood, so absent an unreported step (FIML with covariates modeled, multiple imputation, or a BASIC/AUXILIARY specification), cases missing on any covariate are dropped. Percent free/reduced-price lunch is also a covariate and its coverage is never mentioned at all, even though it is a school-level variable that individual teachers are often unable to report. Missingness on the substantive scales themselves is never reported. The analytic sample is thus not reconstructable from the paper, and the constant N = 5,550 in the table notes is likely a description of the recruited sample rather than of the cases actually estimated.

**Clustering and single-informant issues.** The authors examined a null model and found state-level ICCs of .006–.018, then proceeded without multilevel modeling. State is not the theoretically relevant cluster — administrator support is a property of a school — but the authors are honest that school- and district-level clustering could not be assessed because 'one or two respondents' populate most clusters. That sparseness cuts both ways: it means standard errors are probably not badly understated, but it also means administrator support is measured entirely as one individual's perception, with essentially no within-school replication to separate the principal's actual conduct from the respondent's evaluative disposition. Combined with the fact that all six constructs share a single informant and instrument, this leaves a live and unaddressed common-method channel. There is no marker variable, no method factor, no Harman-type test, and no external anchor such as administrative records. The Limitations section names self-report and social desirability, but frames them as noise rather than as a mechanism that inflates the structural estimates specifically. Mediator–outcome confounding is similarly untreated: the covariate set contains nothing on workload, compensation, class size, school behavioral climate, or personal mental-health history, and trait negative affectivity alone would confound the anxiety → quit path that carries the largest mediated effect in the paper.

**A reporting error worth knowing about.** The Results section states, describing quit intentions, that 'In turn, anxiety/stress was positively related to safety perceptions and was negatively related to quit intentions (see Table 2).' Table 2 reports anxiety/stress → quit intentions at β = +0.25, p < .001, and Table 1 gives the anxiety–safety correlation as −.32. Both halves of that sentence invert the paper's own numbers. It appears to be a drafting error that survived four rounds of revision and copyediting, and it does not affect the estimates, but it is worth noting for anyone reading the narrative rather than the tables.

**Bottom line for a reader.** The trustworthy output of this paper is a large, precisely estimated, cross-sectionally observed correlation structure: teachers who report more administrator support report markedly lower intent to transfer and, to a lesser degree, lower intent to quit; they also report feeling safer and less anxious; and teachers reporting more student-perpetrated victimization report worse on all counts. These patterns are stable across two model specifications and consistent with a substantial prior literature. Everything layered on top of that — the causal ordering, the mediation as mechanism, and above all the moderation that gives the paper its title — rests on choices the design cannot support, on a model that misfits by the paper's own criteria, on a coefficient table whose metric is not interpretable, and on two marginal interaction coefficients whose plotted magnitude is close to nil. Cite the associations, and treat the buffering story as a hypothesis this study raised rather than one it tested.

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper is authoritative and current on its home turf — the violence-against-educators literature, which several of these authors built — but it is thin and occasionally inaccurate everywhere else. Three problems matter most for readers: the opening teacher-attrition statistic is attributed to an NCES report on *principal* attrition; the headline novelty claim about "multi-item latent constructs" is contradicted by the paper's own Methods and rests on a flattening characterization of the two comparison studies; and the paper never states what it adds beyond four or five closely overlapping prior papers from the same team and the same survey. For an Educational Researcher article about principals and teacher retention, the near-total absence of the education-policy and economics-of-education literature on exactly that question (Grissom, Ladd, Kraft, Papay, Simon & Johnson, Grissom/Egalite/Lindsay) is a serious gap in placement.

**Strengths:**

- Genuinely strong and current coverage of the teacher-victimization literature: Longobardi et al. (2019) meta-analysis, Berkowitz et al. (2022), the Moon studies, McMahon et al. (2017) on the ecology of victimization and administrative non-support, and NCES crime-and-safety indicators (Irwin et al., 2023). This is the paper's real scholarly base and it is well handled.
- The intentions-versus-actual-turnover problem is named and cited to the right source. Nguyen et al. (2025, EEPA) appears in both the introduction and the limitations, and the limitations sentence — that intentions are 'distinct from and not a proxy for actual turnover' — is unusually candid for a paper whose entire outcome is intentions.
- The mediation logic (support → safety and anxiety/stress → intentions) is built from a coherent chain of appraisal-oriented citations (Hascher & Waber, 2021; Hascher et al., 2021; Agyapong et al., 2022) rather than asserted, and the construct definition of administrator support is properly sourced (Pohl & Galletta, 2017; Boyd et al., 2011; Martinez & McAbee, 2020).
- Two high-quality syntheses are at least present in the reference list — Liebowitz & Porter (2019, RER) and Borman & Dowling (2008, RER) — and Sorensen & Ladd (2020) supplies a policy-relevant consequence of turnover.

**Weaknesses:**

- Citation error in the first paragraph. The teacher quit/transfer statistics (8% public and 12% private quit; 8% public and 6% private transferred) are attributed to 'Taie & Lewis, 2023,' which the reference list gives as 'Principal attrition and mobility: Results from the 2021–22 Principal Follow-Up Survey ... (NCES 2023-046).' A Principal Follow-Up Survey report cannot supply teacher attrition rates. The same source is invoked again later for 'national concerns about teacher recruitment and retention.' The likely intended source is the parallel NCES Teacher Follow-Up Survey report (also Taie & Lewis, 2023), so this is probably a reference-list error rather than a fabricated number — but as printed, the citation does not support the statistic, and the framing 'quit ... between 2020 and 2022' reads as a two-year rate when TFS reports a one-year rate.
- The central novelty claim is overstated and internally inconsistent. The paper says it is 'one of the first to utilize multi-item latent constructs to measure teachers' perceived victimization and retention intentions.' But the Data Analysis Plan states the structural model used 'composite scores generated from our multi-item latent constructs' — composites, not latent variables — and the Educator Victimization Scale items were explicitly 'dichotomized to represent whether each item occurred at least once (coded as 1) or never (coded as 0)' and scored with KR-20. The paper is therefore using summed binary items for the very construct whose binary measurement it criticizes in others. Separately, multi-item turnover-intention scales are standard, not novel: the paper's own citations to Griffeth et al. (2000), Madigan & Kim (2021), and Johnson (2021) rest on exactly such measures.
- The comparison studies are characterized in a way that flattens them and inverts the actual trade-off. Curran, Viano & Fisher (2019) and Moon, Saw & McCluskey (2020) are dismissed as using 'unvalidated binary indicators.' Both, to my recollection, draw on the federal SASS/Teacher Follow-Up Survey — meaning they measure *actual* transfer and exit behavior on a nationally representative probability sample, not self-reported intentions on a convenience panel. That is a validity advantage on the outcome, and the paper's claim to 'improve upon the analytical precision of past work' does not acknowledge it. Curran et al.'s subtitle ('contextual factors promoting resilience') also suggests it already tested victimization-by-context moderation, which is close to this paper's Research Question 3.
- No account of the increment over the team's own prior work on the same data. The 2020–21 APA Task Force survey has already produced McMahon, Swenski et al. (2024, School Psychology), whose title is 'Teacher-directed violence and anxiety and stress: Predicting intentions to transfer and quit' — the same dataset, the same mediator, the same two outcomes. Add McMahon, Worrell et al. (2024, American Psychologist), which supplied the anxiety/stress, transfer/quit, and victimization scales; Reddy et al. (2024) on safety and well-being; Astor et al. (2024) on policies and relational factors; and Peist et al. (2024) on violence and turnover through a climate framework. All are cited, none is delineated. A reader cannot tell which associations here are new evidence and which are re-analyses of results already in print, and risks double-counting this paper as independent confirmation of its own antecedents.
- The education-policy and economics-of-education literature on principals and teacher retention is essentially absent, which is conspicuous in AERA's flagship general-audience journal. Boyd et al. (2011, AERJ) is cited only for a definition, never for its finding that administrative support is the working condition most predictive of turnover. Missing entirely: Grissom (2011) on whether good principals keep teachers in disadvantaged schools; Ladd (2011, EEPA) on working conditions predicting *planned versus actual* teacher movement — the single most directly relevant education study to this paper's stated limitation; Kraft, Marinell & Shen-Wei Yee (2016); Kraft & Papay (2014); Johnson, Kraft & Papay (2012); Simon & Johnson (2015); and Grissom, Egalite & Lindsay (2021), the field-standard synthesis of how principals affect schools, in which teacher retention is a headline channel. Because that literature is absent, so are its design worries — principal sorting, within-school identification, and the fact that dissatisfied teachers rate their leaders worse — which are precisely what a cross-sectional same-respondent design cannot address.
- Almost no engagement with conflicting or complicating evidence. The review is uniformly confirmatory. There is no acknowledgment of common-method and negative-affectivity concerns, even though the perceived-organizational-support tradition the paper borrows its definition from (via Pohl & Galletta, 2017) has debated them for decades. Liebowitz & Porter's (2019) meta-analysis, which is notably cautious about the causal evidence for principal behaviors, is used for the flat causal claim that feeling supported 'leads to less attrition.' Kapa & Gimbert (2018) on rule enforcement and victimization is cited only for a positive-work-environment generality. And the paper's own unexpected result — anxiety/stress becoming *less* predictive of quit intentions at high victimization — is explained by an unsupported post hoc conjecture with no literature invoked.
- The single citation carrying the paper's headline moderation claim is a small study whose characterization is unverified in text. 'Social support has been found to be negatively related to work stress only for teachers who have not experienced violence (Bounds & Jenkins, 2016)' is the lone direct antecedent for the 'necessary but not sufficient' thesis. Bounds & Jenkins is a modest-sample Contemporary School Psychology article; a reader should not treat one such study as an established buffering-failure literature, particularly since the paper's own results are inconsistent with a clean version of it (the Support × Victimization interaction is significant for quit intentions but null for transfer intentions).
- No named theoretical framework, despite a mediation–moderation design that invites one. Job demands–resources theory, conservation of resources, transactional stress and coping, and Eisenberger's perceived organizational support model would each predict the tested buffering pattern; none is named. The paper substitutes a chain of empirical citations for a theory section.
- Several load-bearing general claims rest on small, non-U.S., low-visibility studies — Ertürk (2021, International Journal of Contemporary Educational Research), Balyer et al. (2017), Sirisookslip et al. (2015, Procedia). Ertürk in particular is used twice for causal-sounding statements about what administrator support does. Meanwhile the most-cited synthesis in the paper, Martinez & McAbee (2020), appears in Education Leadership Review, a lower-circulation outlet, and carries far more of the argument than the RER meta-analysis does.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not repeat the opening attrition statistics from this paper. The reference given (Taie & Lewis, 2023, NCES 2023-046) is the Principal Follow-Up Survey report on principals. Go to the corresponding NCES Teacher Follow-Up Survey report for the 2021–22 teacher attrition and mobility rates, and note that TFS figures are one-year rates, not the 2020-to-2022 span the sentence implies.
- Read this paper alongside McMahon, Swenski et al. (2024, School Psychology, 39[5], 530–544) before citing it as independent evidence. That paper uses the same APA Task Force survey to predict transfer and quit intentions from teacher-directed violence and anxiety/stress. Reddy et al. (2024, same issue), McMahon, Worrell et al. (2024, American Psychologist, 79[7]), Astor et al. (2024, JCP), and Peist et al. (2024) draw on the same or adjacent data. Treat the set as one research program with correlated results, not as five independent confirmations.
- Cite this paper for the moderation finding, not for the measurement claim. The 'one of the first to utilize multi-item latent constructs' assertion is contradicted by the Methods, where victimization items are dichotomized and the structural model runs on composite scores rather than latent variables. If what you want is a latent-variable measurement advance in teacher victimization or retention intentions, this is not the citation.
- Verify the characterization of Curran, Viano & Fisher (2019, Journal of School Violence) and Moon, Saw & McCluskey (2020) before repeating the 'unvalidated binary indicators' framing. Check their data source — I believe both use the federal SASS/Teacher Follow-Up Survey, which means they observe actual turnover on a nationally representative sample. If so, they are stronger, not weaker, than this paper on the outcome side, and Curran et al. likely already tested contextual moderation of the victimization–turnover link.
- For the causal question this paper cannot answer, read the education-policy literature it omits. Ladd (2011, EEPA 33[2]) is the essential companion: it tests working-conditions perceptions against both planned and actual teacher movement and finds school leadership the most predictive domain. Add Grissom (2011, AERJ 48[5]) on principal effectiveness and retention in disadvantaged schools, Kraft, Marinell & Shen-Wei Yee (2016, AERJ), Simon & Johnson (2015, TCR), and Grissom, Egalite & Lindsay (2021, Wallace Foundation) for the synthesis view of how principals affect teacher retention. Boyd et al. (2011, AERJ) — cited here only definitionally — should be read for its findings and its within-school design.
- Treat the 'necessary but not sufficient' framing as a hypothesis with thin antecedent support. Bounds & Jenkins (2016) is the sole prior study cited for it; look at it directly and note that this paper's own moderation is significant for quit intentions but not for transfer intentions, and that one interaction (anxiety/stress × victimization) runs opposite to prediction. The title is stronger than the evidence base behind it, and the design cannot speak to necessity at all.
- Discount the causal-sounding sentences built on Ertürk (2021), Balyer et al. (2017), and Sirisookslip et al. (2015) — small, non-U.S., low-visibility studies used to support general claims about U.S. school administrators. Also check Liebowitz & Porter (2019, RER 89[5]) yourself: my recollection is that this meta-analysis is markedly more cautious about the causal evidence for principal behaviors than the phrase 'leads to less attrition' suggests.
- If you need the theoretical scaffolding the paper leaves implicit, the job demands–resources model and Eisenberger's perceived organizational support tradition (from which the paper's own Pohl & Galletta definition descends) supply the buffering logic being tested — and, importantly, also supply the common-method-variance critique that the paper does not engage.

**Detailed Commentary:**

TRANSPARENCY ABOUT WHAT I VERIFIED. My highest-confidence findings are the ones checkable entirely inside this document, and readers should weight them accordingly: (1) the reference list entry for Taie & Lewis (2023) is a Principal Follow-Up Survey report on principals, while the in-text citation attributes teacher quit and transfer rates to it; (2) the paper claims 'multi-item latent constructs' as its novelty while the Data Analysis Plan says the model used 'composite scores' and the Measures section says victimization items were 'dichotomized'; (3) the paper cites McMahon Swenski et al. (2024), McMahon Worrell et al. (2024), Reddy et al. (2024), Astor et al. (2024), and Peist et al. (2024) without ever stating its increment over any of them; (4) the reference list contains no Grissom, Kraft, Papay, or Simon & Johnson, and Boyd et al. (2011) appears only in a definitional sentence. Those four are established from the text itself. Lower confidence attaches to my recollection of specific external papers — that Curran et al. (2019) and Moon et al. (2020) use SASS/TFS and therefore measure actual turnover, that Ladd (2011) finds leadership the most predictive working condition for both planned and actual movement, that Liebowitz & Porter (2019) is cautious about causal evidence, and the exact form of the Bounds & Jenkins (2016) interaction. Each of those is a 'verify before repeating' item, not an established error.

WHY THE SELF-CITATION PROBLEM IS THE CENTRAL ONE FOR READERS. This is a well-executed research program by scholars who essentially defined the violence-against-educators field in the U.S. But the APA Task Force survey has now generated a series of papers with overlapping constructs, and this article is the fifth or sixth from it that touches transfer and quit intentions. McMahon, Swenski et al. (2024) is the sharpest case: same data, same anxiety/stress mediator, same transfer and quit outcomes, and a title that describes almost the same analysis. The genuine increment here is plausibly (a) adding administrator support as the focal predictor and (b) treating victimization as a moderator rather than a predictor — the discussion gestures at (b) as a contribution. But the paper never says this plainly, and the Study Purpose section instead claims a measurement novelty that does not survive contact with the Methods. The practical risk is a literature that reads five correlated analyses of one 2020–21 convenience sample as five independent studies. Anyone building a meta-analysis or an evidence review on teacher victimization and turnover intentions should map these papers' sample and construct overlap before including them as separate effect sizes.

WHY THE MISSING ECONOMICS AND POLICY LITERATURE CHANGES HOW TO READ THE FINDINGS. Educational Researcher reaches an audience for whom 'do principals affect teacher retention' is a twenty-year-old empirical question with a specific methodological history. That history is about identification: teachers are not randomly assigned to principals, principals are not randomly assigned to schools, and teachers who are dissatisfied for reasons unrelated to leadership rate their leadership worse. Boyd et al. (2011) — cited here — addressed this with panel data and within-school variation. Ladd (2011) addressed the intentions-versus-behavior gap directly. Grissom (2011) addressed the disadvantaged-schools case. Grissom, Egalite & Lindsay (2021) synthesized the whole line. None of that framing appears. The result is that a cross-sectional, single-respondent, single-timepoint association between two self-reported perceptions is presented as advancing knowledge about administrator effects, without situating itself against designs built specifically to rule out the confounds it cannot rule out. This is not an argument that the paper's finding is wrong — the direction is consistent with the policy literature. It is an argument that a reader should not treat the coefficients as effect estimates comparable to that literature, and the paper's own framing does not supply that caution.

HOW THE NOVELTY CLAIM MISDIRECTS. The comparison the paper draws — our validated multi-item scales versus their unvalidated binary indicators — describes a real difference on the predictor side but inverts the trade on the outcome side. SASS/TFS-based studies observe whether a teacher actually left; this study observes whether a teacher agreed with 'I plan to quit my profession or retire early.' The paper itself, citing Nguyen et al. (2025), concedes that only about a third of teachers who want to quit do so, and that intentions are 'not a proxy' for turnover. So the honest positioning is a trade — richer measurement of psychological constructs, weaker measurement of the behavior everyone cares about, on a non-probability panel — rather than an unambiguous improvement in 'analytical precision.' Readers deciding whether to cite this or Curran et al. for a claim about victimization and turnover should choose on that basis, and should note that the two literatures answer different questions.

ONE THING THE PAPER DOES WELL THAT IS EASY TO MISS. The limitations section is more forthright than the introduction. It concedes self-report bias, the intentions-turnover gap with the right citation, retrospective recall contaminated by the COVID shutdown, the inability to model school- or district-level clustering, and differential nonresponse by victimization experience. That list is nearly a complete account of why the estimates should be read as descriptive associations. The problem is one of emphasis: none of those concessions is reflected in the abstract, which uses 'the effect of administrative support,' or in the title's necessity language, or in the Implications section, which recommends specific administrator professional development as though the causal chain were established. Read the limitations section first, then the abstract, and calibrate accordingly.

WHERE THE COVERAGE IS ACTUALLY STRONG. On teacher-directed violence itself, this is close to a complete map of the recent literature: the Longobardi et al. (2019) prevalence meta-analysis, Berkowitz et al. (2022) on socioecological framing of teacher safety, McMahon et al. (2017) on the ecology of victimization and administrative non-support, the two 2020 McMahon papers on verbal and physical aggression antecedents, Reddy et al. (2018) on measurement, and the NCES crime and safety indicators. If you are entering the violence-against-educators literature, this paper's reference list is a usable entry point. It is the bridge to education policy, to the causal-inference tradition, and to the paper's own antecedents that is missing.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper is conventionally organized and easy to navigate — numbered research questions and hypotheses that recur as headings in the Results and Discussion — and its descriptive statistics are internally consistent. But the prose repeatedly disagrees with the exhibits, including a flatly incorrect sentence describing the paper's central mediation result, a Discussion summary that contradicts both Table 3 and its own later paragraph, causal and turnover language the design cannot support, and a 'good fit' claim that fails the paper's own stated criteria. A reader cannot take the narrative on trust; almost every substantive claim needs to be re-derived from Tables 2 and 3.

**Strengths:**

- Standard IMRaD structure with a clear scaffold: three numbered research questions each paired with an explicit hypothesis (p. 3), and matching subheadings in the Data Analysis Plan, Results, and Discussion, so a reader can trace any one question end-to-end without hunting.
- Descriptive reporting is clean and verifiable: every demographic breakdown in the Participants section (gender, race/ethnicity, school level, urbanicity) sums exactly to N = 5,550, and Table 1's correlations are consistent with the directional claims in the Results' first paragraph.
- The Limitations section (p. 10) is unusually candid for a paper of this type — it explicitly states the data are 'methodologically cross-sectional,' that intentions are 'distinct from and not a proxy for actual turnover' (citing Nguyen et al., 2025), that clustering below the state level could not be assessed, and that victimized teachers may be differentially likely to have responded.
- The Discussion's Moderating Effects paragraph (p. 9) does the honest thing in one place — 'moderated the relations among administrator support, anxiety/stress, and intentions to quit (but not transfer)' — and openly labels the anxiety/stress × victimization result as 'one unexpected finding' rather than burying it.
- Measures are described item-by-item with verbatim item text, response anchors, and reliabilities, so a reader can judge construct coverage without chasing the source instruments.

**Weaknesses:**

- The mediation paragraph's summary sentence (p. 6) is simply wrong: 'anxiety/stress was positively related to safety perceptions and was negatively related to quit intentions (see Table 2).' Table 2 (p. 8) reports anxiety/stress → quit intentions as beta = +0.25, and there is no anxiety → safety path in the model at all (they are parallel mediators); Table 1 puts their correlation at -.32. Both clauses of the sentence a reader would quote for the mediation result contradict the table it cites.
- The Discussion's opening summary (p. 9) states that victimization moderated the relations between administrator support and 'transfer and quit intentions.' Table 3 shows all three transfer-intention interactions null (Support × Victimization beta = -0.02, p = .64; Anxiety × Victimization beta = 0.04, p = .38; Safety × Victimization beta = -0.09, p = .11). Two paragraphs later the same Discussion says 'but not transfer.' The paper contradicts itself on its headline moderation finding.
- Results p. 9: 'Teachers with higher rates of victimization were very likely to quit teaching, and administrator support did little to buffer this.' The outcome is a five-point intentions scale, not quitting; 'very likely' is an absolute-risk statement the model never estimates; and Table 3's victimization main effect on quit intentions is not even significant (beta = 0.12, p = .19). Three separate overreaches in one sentence.
- Fit is asserted against criteria the paper itself sets and then fails. Methods (p. 3) specify RMSEA < .05, CFI > .95, SRMR < .08. The mediation model is described as having 'good fit' at RMSEA = .08 and CFI = .91 (p. 5), and the moderation model as 'also had good fit' at RMSEA = .05 and CFI = .93. The pre-emptive McNeish caveat covers only an elevated RMSEA 'when occurring with values in acceptable ranges for all other indices' — CFI = .91 is not in acceptable range, so the escape clause does not apply to the model it is used to defend.
- 'Latent construct' framing versus composite-score analysis. The Study Purpose (p. 3) claims the study 'is one of the first to utilize multi-item latent constructs' and the keyword list includes 'structural equation modeling,' but the Data Analysis Plan (p. 5) says structural relations 'were assessed with composite scores generated from our multi-item latent constructs' — a self-contradictory phrase. This is path analysis on observed composites; measurement error is not modeled in the structural estimates, and the victimization composite is a count of dichotomized items. The claimed methodological advance over 'unvalidated binary indicators' is thinner than the framing implies.
- Abstract fidelity. It says the authors 'examined the effect of administrative support' — causal language the Limitations explicitly disclaim — and reports that victimization 'weakened the relationship between administrator support and retention intentions,' generalizing to both outcomes an interaction significant only for quit. It omits that the design is cross-sectional, that all measures are self-report, that outcomes are intentions rather than turnover, that recruitment was an opt-in email/partner-distribution sample during COVID-19, and the paper's own 'unexpected' opposite-signed finding. It contains no numbers at all.
- The Methods claim outcomes were measured at survey completion 'thus establishing causal order for the primary analyses' (p. 4), which the Limitations section on p. 10 flatly retracts. Compounding this, the administrator support scale is the one measure given no reference period, so the timing logic the causal-order claim rests on is unstated for the paper's key predictor.
- Table 3's victimization main effects (beta = -1.69 for anxiety/stress, beta = -1.74 for safety) are labelled standardized betas with no explanatory note. They lie far outside the plausible range a reader associates with standardized coefficients, and the anxiety sign is opposite to Table 1's r = +.36. These are artifacts of standardizing a model containing product terms built with Mplus's DEFINE, but nothing in the table, note, or text says so.
- Figure 1 silently merges two different models. Its five main-effect coefficients (.28, -.19, -.36, -.23, and the mediator-to-outcome paths) come from Table 2, while the four dead-end arrows from Teacher Victimization (-.42, .39, .12, -.12) are interaction terms from Table 3. There is no key distinguishing them. The note claims 'Nonsignificant and covariate estimates are not presented,' yet the two highly significant victimization main effects (p < .001) appear nowhere, and the Support × Victimization → anxiety path reads .39 in the figure against 0.40 in Table 3.
- Figure 2 (p. 7) has no axis titles on any of four panels, four different y-axis ranges, and an x-axis running -1.1 to 1.1 in unlabelled units. Despite the 'simple slope analyses' caption these are not conventional simple-slope plots (predicted outcome by predictor at levels of the moderator) but plots of the conditional slope against the moderator with confidence bands — a reader expecting the former will misread all four. The caption also carries an uncorrected production error: '(b) 2b.' and '(c) 2c.'
- The title's 'Necessary but Not Sufficient' is a framing the evidence does not deliver. Necessity is untestable in this design, and 'not sufficient' rests on two interaction coefficients of magnitude 0.12 at p = .02 in a sample of 5,550; Figure 2c shows the support–quit slope moving only from roughly -.33 to -.31 across the plotted range of victimization and never approaching zero. The exhibit undercuts the prose's 'did little to buffer this' and 'benefited the least.'
- Construct-label polarity is unstable. 'Retention intentions' is used as the umbrella for two measured variables that are intentions to LEAVE, so Hypothesis 3's 'weaken the positive associations between administrator support, safety, and retention intentions' is coherent only under the staying reading while every table coefficient is on the leaving reading. Hypothesis 3 also predicts victimization would 'strengthen the negative role of anxiety/stress' when the model parameterizes anxiety as positively related to quitting and the finding runs the opposite way.
- Smaller frictions that add up: the victimization scale is called '5-point' and then anchored '0 (never) to 5 (daily),' which is six points (p. 4); Table 1 carries no note on metrics, so a reader may compare victimization's M = 2.52 (a 0–11 count of dichotomies) directly to anxiety's M = 2.73 (a 1–5 mean); neither Table 2 nor Table 3 reports fit indices, R-squared, or covariate estimates, so the tables are not self-contained; and the Results for RQ3 interpret main effects ('All previously reported associations remained significant... magnitude of all effects remaining consistent') after the Methods stated 'Main effects were not interpreted in this second iteration.'

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not quote the mediation paragraph on p. 6. Its closing sentence misstates the sign of the anxiety/stress → quit path and invents an anxiety → safety path. Read Table 2 (p. 8) instead: support → anxiety = -0.19, support → safety = 0.28, anxiety → transfer = 0.14, anxiety → quit = 0.25, safety → transfer = -0.17, safety → quit = -0.11, and the four indirect effects range from -0.03 to -0.05. The correct verbal summary is that supported teachers report less anxiety and more safety, and both of those in turn track lower intent to leave.
- Before repeating the moderation finding, check Table 3's p-values yourself. Only four of the twelve interaction terms are significant, and all four involve quit intentions or the mediators — every transfer-intention interaction is null. The Discussion's opening summary claims moderation of 'transfer and quit intentions'; the correct version is the paper's own later parenthetical, 'but not transfer.'
- Treat every 'effect,' 'influence,' 'lead to,' and 'quit teaching' in the Abstract, Results, and Discussion as shorthand for a cross-sectional association with an intentions scale. Read the Limitations section on p. 10 first — it is where the paper states the design constraints the Abstract omits — and read the whole paper against it.
- The Results sentence 'Teachers with higher rates of victimization were very likely to quit teaching' should not be cited. Table 3 reports victimization's main effect on quit intentions as beta = 0.12, p = .19, and the outcome is an intentions scale, not turnover.
- For magnitude, go to Figure 2, not the prose. Panels (a) and (b) show the substantive attenuation — the support–anxiety slope moving from about -.19 to -.13 and the support–safety slope from about .22 to .165 across the moderator range. Panels (c) and (d), the two the title's argument rests on, are nearly flat. Note the panels use four different y-axis ranges and no axis labels, so read the values, not the visual steepness, and do not compare panels by eye.
- Do not try to interpret Table 3's victimization main effects (-1.69, -1.74) as standardized coefficients. They are standardization artifacts in a model containing product terms; the -1.69 even reverses the sign of Table 1's victimization–anxiety correlation (+.36). Treat the interaction terms and the direct paths as the interpretable content of that table.
- When reading Figure 1, identify each coefficient's source before using it. The five arrows into and out of the mediators are Table 2 (no-interaction) estimates; the four arrows that terminate mid-air pointing at other paths are Table 3 interaction terms. Anything you plan to cite should be pulled from the tables, not the diagram — the Support × Victimization → anxiety path prints as .39 in the figure and 0.40 in Table 3.
- Read 'latent constructs' and the 'structural equation modeling' keyword as the paper's framing, not its method. The Data Analysis Plan on p. 5 is the authoritative sentence: composite scores in a path model. If measurement error matters to your use of these estimates, the reported coefficients are attenuated relative to a true latent-variable model.
- Watch the polarity of 'retention intentions.' It labels two scales on which a higher score means more intent to leave, so a negative coefficient means support is associated with staying. Hypothesis 3's wording assumes the opposite polarity; the tables use the leaving polarity throughout.
- Efficient reading path: Abstract (with skepticism), Study Purpose and the three hypotheses (p. 3), Data Analysis Plan (p. 5, which is where the fit statistics and the covariate list live — they are in no table), Tables 2 and 3 (p. 8), Figure 2 (p. 7), Limitations (p. 10). The introduction and literature review (pp. 1–3) restate widely known findings on administrator support and turnover and can be skimmed. The Implications for Education Practice and Research section (pp. 10–11) is largely programmatic recommendations about professional development, MTSS, and discipline policy that are not derived from any estimate in this paper, and can be skipped by anyone reading for evidence.
- One item that does check out: the Methods' 'the measurement model described last' is accurate — the Measurement model subsection is genuinely the last of the Measures subsections (p. 4). It reads oddly because it is dropped into a fit-criteria sentence before the reader knows the section order, but it is not an error.

**Detailed Commentary:**

ORGANIZATION AND NAVIGABILITY. The article is easy to move around in. Three research questions, each immediately followed by its hypothesis, are laid out on p. 3; the Data Analysis Plan (p. 5) states which model addresses which question; the Results uses three subheadings that map one-to-one onto RQ1, RQ2, and RQ3; and the Discussion's 'Benefits of Administrator Support' and 'Moderating Effects of Teacher Victimization' preserve that order. A reader wanting only the moderation story can go directly to Results p. 9, Table 3 on p. 8, and Figure 2 on p. 7. Measures are given with verbatim items, anchors, and alphas, which is genuinely useful. The problem is not structure; it is that the sentences inside the structure repeatedly do not match the exhibits.

THE CENTRAL PROSE ERROR (p. 6).
