The Mediation of Teacher Safety and Anxiety/Stress paragraph builds correctly for four sentences and then closes: 'The more teachers felt supported by their administrators, the less they felt anxious and stressed and the more they felt safe. In turn, anxiety/stress was positively related to safety perceptions and was negatively related to quit intentions (see Table 2).' Neither clause survives contact with Table 2. Anxiety/stress → quit intentions is beta = 0.25, SE = 0.01, 95% CI [0.22, 0.28] — positive, and one of the largest paths in the model. And no anxiety → safety path exists: the two are specified as parallel mediators of administrator support, and Table 1 gives their zero-order correlation as -.32, the opposite sign from the sentence's 'positively related.' The sentence appears to be a garbled compression of 'administrator support was negatively related to anxiety/stress and positively related to safety perceptions, and safety was negatively related to quit intentions.' Because this is the paragraph that states the paper's mediation result in words, and because the paper's own preceding Results paragraph gets the same relations right ('Anxiety/stress was positively related to both intentions to transfer and quit'), a reader who trusts the narrative will come away with the mechanism inverted.

A SELF-CONTRADICTING DISCUSSION. The Discussion's summary paragraph (p. 9) says: 'Finally, teacher victimization moderated the relations between administrator support and teacher safety, anxiety/stress, and transfer and quit intentions such that the benefits of positive administrator support were reduced when teachers faced victimization by students.' Table 3 says otherwise for transfer intentions on every count: Support × Victimization beta = -0.02, p = .64; Anxiety/Stress × Victimization beta = 0.04, p = .38; Safety × Victimization beta = -0.09, p = .11. Not one transfer-intention interaction is significant. Two paragraphs later, under Moderating Effects, the paper writes 'intentions to quit (but not transfer)' — the accurate version. The paper therefore states both the correct and the incorrect claim within a page, and the incorrect one occupies the summary position readers are most likely to lift.

CLAIMS THE DESIGN CANNOT SUPPORT. Three places overreach in the same direction. (a) Results p. 9: 'Teachers with higher rates of victimization were very likely to quit teaching, and administrator support did little to buffer this.' The outcome is a five-point agreement scale about wanting or planning to quit; 'very likely to quit teaching' is a probability of an event the study never observes; and Table 3's victimization main effect on quit intentions is beta = 0.12, p = .19 — not significant. (b) Discussion p. 9: 'unless victimization against teachers is reduced or eliminated, teachers will be more likely to leave the profession' — a counterfactual claim from cross-sectional associations. (c) The Abstract's 'we examined the effect of administrative support.' All three are contradicted by the paper's own Limitations (p. 10): 'these data are methodologically cross-sectional, limiting our ability to determine the temporal order among variables or make causal inferences.' The Methods add a fourth: 'at the time of survey completion (August 2020–June 2021), thus establishing causal order for the primary analyses' (p. 4). Note also that administrator support — the exposure the whole causal-order argument is about — is the only measure with no reference period specified, while safety, anxiety/stress, and victimization are all anchored to the 2019–2020 pre-COVID year.

FIT REPORTING. The Measures preamble (p. 3) commits to RMSEA < .05, CFI > .95, SRMR < .08 (Hu & Bentler, 1999) and adds one escape clause: elevated RMSEA is acceptable 'when occurring with values in acceptable ranges for all other indices.' The measurement model meets this (RMSEA = .04, CFI = .95, SRMR = .04). The mediation model does not: RMSEA = .08, 90% CI [.08, .09], CFI = .91, SRMR = .02 — the RMSEA is elevated and the CFI is below the stated threshold, so the escape clause does not cover it, yet the text says 'This model had good fit to the data' (p. 5). The moderation model (RMSEA = .05, CFI = .93, SRMR = .04) 'also had good fit,' again with a CFI below the paper's own cutoff. A reader skimming Methods will register 'good fit' twice without noticing that the paper failed the test it set itself.

MEASUREMENT FRAMING. The Study Purpose (p. 3) rests the paper's novelty claim on being 'one of the first to utilize multi-item latent constructs to measure teachers' perceived victimization and retention intentions,' contrasted against prior work's 'unvalidated binary indicators.' The Data Analysis Plan (p. 5) then reveals that the structural model runs on 'composite scores generated from our multi-item latent constructs' — a phrase that cannot mean anything precise. A measurement CFA was fit and reported, but the structural estimates are ordinary path coefficients among observed composites; measurement error is not carried into them. Further, the victimization composite is a sum of eleven items each dichotomized to 0/1 (KR-20 = .79) — closer to the binary indicators the paper criticizes than the framing suggests, though summed rather than single-item. Footnote 1 reports a sensitivity check using 'a composite score version based on the mean average of the original response scale' with unchanged results, which is reassuring but adds a third sense of 'composite' to the paper.

ABSTRACT FIDELITY. Readers who stop at the abstract will get: a causal verb ('the effect of administrative support'); a moderation result generalized from quit intentions to 'retention intentions,' when the Support × Victimization interaction is significant only for quit (beta = 0.12, p = .02) and null for transfer (beta = -0.02, p = .64); and no mention of the fourth significant interaction — the anxiety/stress × victimization effect that ran opposite to Hypothesis 3 and that the Results themselves flag as 'unexpectedly.' The abstract also omits the design entirely: cross-sectional, all self-report, outcomes are intentions rather than turnover, and the sample is an opt-in survey distributed through a commercial contact list and union/association partners during COVID-19 rather than a probability sample — 'a national sample of 5,550 pre-K–12th-grade teachers' invites a representativeness reading the Procedures section does not support (it reports only that demographics 'were comparable to national statistics'). No effect size appears anywhere in the abstract.

HYPOTHESIS–FINDING MISMATCH. Hypothesis 3 predicts victimization will 'weaken the positive associations between administrator support, safety, and retention intentions and strengthen the negative role of anxiety/stress.' The finding is the reverse for anxiety: 'the positive association between anxiety and quit intentions was weakened as victimization reports increased' (p. 9, beta = -0.12, p = .02). The hypothesis is also internally awkward — it calls anxiety's role 'negative' while the model consistently estimates anxiety as positively related to leaving. The same polarity confusion runs through 'retention intentions' as an umbrella term for two scales measuring intent to leave, so 'positive associations between administrator support... and retention intentions' in H3 is coherent only under a staying reading while every coefficient in Tables 2 and 3 is on the leaving reading. The Results and Discussion do handle the unexpected result honestly when they reach it — the Discussion offers a plausible interpretation (anxiety may be relieved by 'the certainty of planning to leave') — but the Discussion's summary sentence and the abstract both smooth it away.

EXHIBITS. Table 1 (p. 5) has a note reading only 'N = 5,550. *p < .001' — no metric information, so the reader cannot tell that variables 1–5 are 1–5 scale means while variable 6 is a 0–11 count of dichotomized items, and may read M = 2.52 for victimization as comparable to M = 2.73 for anxiety. Table 2 and Table 3 (both p. 8) carry no fit indices, no R-squared, and no covariate estimates, so neither is self-contained: model fit lives only in the Data Analysis Plan prose on p. 5, and the demographic and school-level covariate coefficients are never reported anywhere in the article. Table 3's victimization main effects, beta = -1.69 [-1.79, -1.59] for anxiety/stress and beta = -1.74 [-1.83, -1.66] for safety, are presented in a column headed 'beta' with no note; besides lying well outside the range readers associate with standardized coefficients, the anxiety one reverses the sign of Table 1's victimization–anxiety correlation (r = +.36). These are standardization artifacts of a model containing DEFINE-generated product terms, but the reader is told nothing and left to conclude either that victimization strongly reduces anxiety or that something is wrong with the table.

Figure 1 (p. 6) is a single path diagram that mixes two models. Tracing it against the tables: .28 (support → safety), -.19 (support → anxiety), -.36 (support → transfer), -.23 (support → quit), -.17, -.11, .14, .25 are all Table 2 estimates, while the four arrows fanning from Teacher Victimization and terminating mid-air on other paths — -.42, .39, .12, -.12 — are Table 3 interaction terms. Nothing in the caption ('Results of structural models') or the note distinguishes them, and the corresponding Table 3 main-effect versions of the same paths differ (support → safety is .23, not .28; support → quit is -.26, not -.23). The note states 'Nonsignificant and covariate estimates are not presented for clarity,' but the two victimization main effects are significant at p < .001 and still absent — so the note does not describe what was actually omitted. The Support × Victimization → anxiety path is printed as .39 in the figure against 0.40 in Table 3.

Figure 2 (p. 7) is four stacked panels with no axis titles anywhere, four different y-axis ranges (-0.25 to 0.01; 0 to 0.26; 0 to -0.42; 0 to 0.46), and an x-axis of unlabelled units running roughly -1.1 to 1.1. The caption calls them 'simple slope analyses,' but what is plotted is the conditional slope as a function of the moderator with confidence bands, not the conventional two- or three-line simple-slopes plot of the outcome against the predictor. The caption also retains an uncorrected editing artifact — '(b) 2b. Administrator Support × Victimization relating to safety. (c) 2c. Administrator Support × Victimization relating to quit intentions.' Read for content rather than shape, the figure is the most useful exhibit in the paper and quietly undercuts its rhetoric: panels (a) and (b) show real attenuation (the support–anxiety slope from roughly -.19 to -.13, the support–safety slope from roughly .22 to .165), while panel (c) — the one supporting 'administrator support did little to buffer this' and the title's 'not sufficient' — shows the support–quit slope moving only from about -.33 to -.31 and never approaching zero across the plotted range.

TITLE. 'Necessary but Not Sufficient' promises more than the design can deliver in both halves. Necessity cannot be established by a correlational main effect. 'Not sufficient' rests on two interaction terms of magnitude 0.12 at p = .02 in N = 5,550, and on Figure 2c, which shows the buffering benefit of support persisting essentially undiminished at high victimization. The Conclusions section is more careful than the title — 'administrator support, although helpful, may not fully prevent the consequences of such events and could have weaker associations' — and a reader should take that hedged sentence as the paper's actual claim.

DENSITY AND WHAT TO SKIP. The Results occupy roughly a page and a half; the Discussion, Limitations, and Implications together run about four. The Implications for Education Practice and Research section (pp. 10–11) recommends administrator professional development, an MTSS framework, peer mentoring, and clearer discipline policy — none of which follows from any estimate in this paper; the one paragraph that does connect to the data is the observation that one of the three administrator-support items concerns discipline. The Introduction and literature review (pp. 1–3) rehearse familiar findings on administrator support, teacher well-being, and violence against teachers, and can be skimmed for the citations. The material a reader must not skip is the Data Analysis Plan on p. 5 (the only place fit statistics, the ICC check, and the covariate list appear), Tables 2 and 3, Figure 2, and the Limitations. One item on my checklist survived: 'All analyses (including the measurement model described last) were conducted in Mplus' (p. 3) is accurate — the Measurement model subsection is indeed the last subsection of Measures — though it is confusing on first encounter because the reader does not yet know the section order.

SMALLER FRICTIONS. The victimization measure is introduced as 'a 5-point frequency scale, from 0 (never) to 5 (daily)' (p. 4), which is six points. 'Anxiety/stress,' 'anxiety and stress,' and bare 'anxiety' alternate across the text and between Table 2 ('DV: Anxiety') and Table 3 ('DV: Anxiety/stress'). The Methods state 'Main effects were not interpreted in this second iteration of the mediation model' (p. 5), but the Results for RQ3 open by interpreting exactly that: 'All previously reported associations remained significant, with the direction and magnitude of all effects remaining consistent' (p. 9) — which is roughly but not exactly true, since safety → quit falls from -0.11 to -0.08 and support → safety from 0.28 to 0.23.

BOTTOM LINE FOR READERS. The findings themselves are plausible and the tables contain what is needed to state them correctly. But between the abstract, the mediation paragraph, the Discussion summary, the fit claims, and the two figures, there are enough places where the prose says something the exhibits do not that the narrative cannot be relied on as a description of the results. Cite this paper from Tables 2 and 3, not from its sentences.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

Using the 2020–21 APA Task Force national survey of 5,550 pre-K–12 teachers, this paper repositions perceived administrator support as the focal predictor of transfer and quit intentions, tests perceived safety and anxiety/stress as parallel mediators, and — its genuine novelty — treats student-perpetrated victimization as a moderator rather than a predictor. The correlational core is solid and worth citing: administrator support is among the strongest single correlates of transfer intentions (β = −0.36) and quit intentions (β = −0.23) net of safety, anxiety/stress, and demographics. The moderation result that carries the title is the paper's weakest-supported and most quotable claim: the paper's own Figure 2 shows the protective slope of administrator support attenuating only modestly and never approaching zero across the plotted range of victimization, which does not sustain 'necessary but not sufficient' or 'administrator support did little to buffer this.'

**Strengths:**

- Large national sample (N = 5,550) recruited with stratification across region, level, role, and urbanicity, with demographics broadly matching NCES teacher characteristics — one of the largest datasets available on teacher victimization and retention intentions.
- A real conceptual increment over prior work on the same survey: prior team papers treated victimization as a predictor of anxiety/stress and transfer/quit intentions (McMahon, Swenski et al., 2024) or reported national descriptives (McMahon, Worrell et al., 2024); here victimization is repositioned as a moderating context. The closing observation that victimization is 'typically examined as an independent variable or outcome' and is better read as a condition is the paper's most portable idea.
- Measurement is a genuine improvement over the binary victimization/turnover indicators used in comparable large-scale work (Curran et al., 2019; Moon et al., 2020): multi-item scales with reported alphas (.83–.90), a fitted measurement model (RMSEA = .04, CFI = .95, SRMR = .04), and a sensitivity check confirming the dichotomize-and-sum victimization score against a mean composite.
- An underplayed but useful quantitative result: the indirect effects through safety and anxiety/stress (−0.03 to −0.05) are an order of magnitude smaller than the direct effects (−0.23 to −0.36). Roughly 85–90% of the support–intention association does not run through perceived safety or anxiety/stress, which is informative about where the mechanism is not.
- A frank and fairly complete limitations section: self-report, intentions rather than turnover (citing Nguyen et al., 2025 against treating them as proxies), cross-sectional design precluding causal inference, inability to model school/district clustering, and possible victimization-related nonresponse.
- Published in Educational Researcher, so the framing will reach a policy and practitioner audience that the team's prior School Psychology and American Psychologist papers on the same data did not.

**Weaknesses:**

- The title claim is not tested. 'Necessary' is a counterfactual claim no cross-sectional correlational design can support, and 'not sufficient' is established only in the trivial sense that support does not explain all variance. Nothing in the results distinguishes 'support is necessary but insufficient' from 'support and victimization are two largely independent correlates of retention intentions.'
- The moderation results are statistically significant but substantively small, and the paper's prose overstates them. Figure 2c shows the support→quit slope moving from about −0.33 to about −0.30 across the plotted victimization range; Figure 2a shows support→anxiety moving from about −0.19 to −0.13; Figure 2b shows support→safety from about 0.22 to 0.17. In every panel the slope stays strongly in the protective direction and its confidence band never crosses zero. 'Teachers with higher rates of victimization were very likely to quit teaching, and administrator support did little to buffer this' is not what these figures show.
- The interaction model's parameterization is not transparently interpretable, which matters because it is the source of the novel finding. In Table 3 the victimization main effects are reported as standardized β = −1.69 (anxiety) and −1.74 (safety) — outside the standardized range, and the anxiety coefficient is opposite in sign to the zero-order correlation (r = +.36). The authors sidestep this by declining to interpret main effects in the moderation model, but the interaction terms come from the same model and inherit the same scaling.
- Substantial construct overlap with the team's own prior outputs from this survey (McMahon, Swenski et al., 2024; McMahon, Worrell et al., 2024; Reddy et al., 2024; Astor et al., 2024). The anxiety/stress → transfer/quit pathway and the victimization descriptives are already published; the increment is a re-specification of a largely overlapping variable set rather than new evidence.
- Single-informant, single-instrument design across every construct. Perceived administrator support, perceived safety, anxiety/stress, victimization, and intentions all come from the same teacher on the same survey, so common-method variance and a general workplace-negativity halo are live alternative accounts for the entire path structure. Reverse causation is equally consistent with the data: teachers already planning to leave may rate their principal worse.
- Temporal-ordering claims are stronger than the data. The paper says measuring intentions 'at the time of survey completion' establishes causal order, but the administrator support items carry no time referent, mediators and victimization are retrospective reports about 2019–20 collected at the same sitting as the outcomes, and the limitations section correctly concedes the design is 'methodologically cross-sectional.'
- The outcome is partly a pandemic construct. One of three items in each retention subscale is explicitly COVID-framed ('COVID-19 has increased my desire to transfer/quit'), and the mediators reference pre-COVID 2019–20 while outcomes reference August 2020–June 2021 — so the mediation is estimated across a historical discontinuity with a COVID-loaded dependent variable.
- 'National sample' is doing more work than the sampling supports: a purchased marketing-firm email list plus union and association distribution including social-media links, with no reported response rate, no sampling frame denominator, and no weights. Demographic similarity to NCES benchmarks does not address selection on victimization or on retention intentions, which the authors themselves flag.
- The practice implications (administrator professional development, MTSS-framed supports, discipline-policy reform, peer mentoring) are not tested by anything in the study. No PD, policy, or intervention variable is measured; a single item on the three-item support scale mentions discipline, and the discipline-policy discussion rests entirely on prior qualitative work rather than these results.
- The paper claims to be 'one of the first to utilize multi-item latent constructs,' but the structural models were fitted to composite scores rather than latent variables, so measurement error is not modeled in the paths being reported.
- There is an internal inconsistency in the results narration: the mediation section states that 'anxiety/stress was positively related to safety perceptions and was negatively related to quit intentions,' which contradicts both Table 1 (r = −.32 with safety) and Table 2 (anxiety → quit = +0.25).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the magnitude and relative ranking of perceived administrator support as a correlate of teacher retention intentions in a large national teacher sample — support is more strongly associated with transfer intentions (β = −0.36) than either perceived safety (−0.17) or anxiety/stress (0.14), net of demographics and school characteristics.
- CITE IT FOR: the finding that safety and anxiety/stress mediate only a small fraction of the administrator-support/retention-intention association (indirect effects −0.03 to −0.05 against direct effects of −0.23 to −0.36). This is arguably the paper's most useful and most underplayed result, and it argues against well-being-only theories of why supportive principals retain teachers.
- CITE IT FOR: the descriptive picture that teachers reporting more student-perpetrated victimization report markedly lower safety, higher anxiety/stress, and higher transfer and quit intentions during 2020–21 (zero-order rs of .25 to −.36).
- CITE IT FOR: the framing argument that teacher victimization is better treated as a moderating context than as a predictor or outcome — as an agenda-setting proposal and proof of feasibility, not as settled evidence about the size of that moderation.
- DO NOT lean on it for: a causal effect of administrator support on retention. The abstract's word 'effect' is not earned — every construct is self-reported by the same teacher at one sitting, and reverse causation and negativity halo are unaddressed.
- DO NOT lean on it for: the claim that administrator support fails victimized teachers, or for 'necessary but not sufficient.' Figure 2 shows the support slope attenuating by roughly 10% (quit intentions) to 30% (anxiety) across the plotted victimization range while remaining strongly protective throughout — the figure argues the opposite of the title.
- DO NOT lean on it for: the moderation coefficients as effect sizes. The interaction model reports standardized victimization main effects of −1.69 and −1.74 that fall outside the standardized range and, for anxiety, reverse the sign of the bivariate correlation, so the interaction terms from that model should not be read at face value.
- DO NOT lean on it for: actual teacher turnover. The outcomes are intentions, one of three items in each scale explicitly names COVID-19, and the paper itself cites Nguyen et al. (2025) warning that intentions are not a turnover proxy.
- DO NOT lean on it for: national prevalence of victimization, administrator support, or attrition intent. The sample is a non-probability convenience sample with no reported response rate or weights; use McMahon, Worrell et al. (2024) or NCES sources for descriptives, and note that even those carry the same sampling caveat.
- DO NOT lean on it for: current or post-pandemic conditions, or for the 'unexpected' finding that anxiety/stress predicts quitting less strongly among highly victimized teachers. That result rests on a p = .02 interaction in a model whose parameterization is questionable, and the authors' explanation (relief from having decided to leave) is post hoc.
- OPEN QUESTIONS a reader should carry forward: whether any of these associations survive longitudinal or administrative-data designs linking principal support to realized turnover; whether the support × victimization interaction replicates outside the pandemic window and outside single-informant data; what administrators actually do, given that 'support' here is three perception items; whether the moderation is large enough anywhere in the victimization distribution to change practice; and whether reducing victimization improves retention, which the design cannot address.
- POSITIONING: on the general question of whether principal support relates to teacher retention, this does not displace administrative-data and panel work (e.g., Boyd et al., 2011) and should be read as corroborating rather than best-available evidence. On the narrower question of whether victimization conditions the value of administrator support, it is currently the largest and most explicit test in the U.S. literature — which makes it the natural citation on that question and also means the question is essentially untested by anyone else.

**Detailed Commentary:**

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW. This is at least the fifth publication drawing on the 2020–21 APA Task Force survey by an overlapping author team, and the paper's own reference list makes the overlap easy to trace: McMahon, Swenski et al. (2024) already estimated victimization and anxiety/stress predicting transfer and quit intentions in this dataset; McMahon, Worrell et al. (2024) reported the national descriptives on violence, retention, stress, and training needs; Reddy et al. (2024) analyzed safety and well-being; Astor et al. (2024) analyzed policies and relational factors predicting victimization and safety. Against that backdrop the increment here is narrow but real, and consists of two moves: (1) promoting perceived administrator support from background covariate to focal predictor with safety and anxiety/stress as parallel mediators, and (2) demoting victimization from predictor to moderator of the whole path structure. The second move is the more interesting of the two, and the discussion is right that victimization is usually modeled as a cause or an outcome rather than as a condition. Readers should treat that reframing as the paper's durable contribution, more so than any specific coefficient it reports.

THE GAP BETWEEN THE QUOTABLE AND THE SUPPORTED. This paper has an unusually clean case of the most-cited claim not being the best-supported one, and the divergence is visible within the paper itself. The title asserts 'Necessary but Not Sufficient'; the discussion says 'teachers with higher rates of student violence benefited the least from administrators' support'; the results say 'teachers with higher rates of victimization were very likely to quit teaching, and administrator support did little to buffer this.' Figure 2 does not show this. Panel (c) — the panel that most directly speaks to the quit claim — shows the administrator-support slope on quit intentions moving from roughly −0.33 at the low end of the plotted victimization range to roughly −0.30 at the high end, with the confidence band comfortably below zero throughout. Panel (a) shows support→anxiety moving from about −0.19 to −0.13; panel (b) shows support→safety from about 0.22 to about 0.17; panel (d) shows anxiety→quit from about 0.38 to about 0.35. In no panel does the slope reach zero, change sign, or lose significance anywhere in the range plotted. The honest summary of Figure 2 is that administrator support retains most of its association with better outcomes even among highly victimized teachers, with modest attenuation. A reader who cites this paper for 'administrator support does not help victimized teachers' will be citing it for the reverse of what its own figures show. Note also the asymmetry the abstract elides: for transfer intentions — the outcome with the largest support coefficient — none of the three interaction terms is significant at all (p = .64, .38, .11), and the quit-intention moderations are p = .02. Only the two mediator-outcome moderations (support × victimization on anxiety, +0.40, and on safety, −0.42) reach p < .001, and those concern mediators rather than the retention outcomes the title is about.

A PARAMETERIZATION PROBLEM UNDER THE HEADLINE RESULT. Table 3 reports the victimization main effect as standardized β = −1.69 on anxiety/stress and −1.74 on safety. Standardized path coefficients of that magnitude are not impossible in models with correlated predictors, but −1.69 on anxiety is also opposite in sign to the zero-order correlation in Table 1 (r = +.36), and both values are far outside anything the mediation model in Table 2 produces. The authors' response is to state that 'main effects were not interpreted in this second iteration' — but the interaction coefficients they do interpret come from the same fit, share the same centering and scaling of the product terms, and are large relative to everything else in the model (+0.40, −0.42). Readers should treat the interaction magnitudes as directional evidence at best; the simple-slope figure, which is on an interpretable scale, is the more trustworthy summary and is the one that undercuts the headline. The paper does not report whether the moderator was mean-centered or standardized before forming products, nor does it report a change in fit or variance explained from adding the interactions, both of which would have been the natural diagnostics.

AN UNDERPLAYED RESULT THAT DESERVES CITATION. The mediation results are more informative than the paper makes them. Indirect effects run −0.03 to −0.05 while direct effects run −0.23 to −0.36, meaning roughly 85–90% of the association between perceived administrator support and retention intentions does not pass through perceived safety or anxiety/stress. The discussion reads this as confirming that safety and anxiety/stress 'serve as mechanisms,' which is technically true but badly proportioned: the finding is that these two well-being channels account for very little of the relationship. That is a genuinely useful negative result for a literature that often assumes principal support works on retention by improving teacher well-being, and readers building theory in this space should cite it in that direction rather than as mediation confirmation.

GENERALIZABILITY AND BOUNDARY-DRAWING. The limitations section is candid about the big three (self-report, intentions not turnover, cross-sectional) and even about differential nonresponse by victimization status, which is to the authors' credit. But two boundaries are drawn less honestly elsewhere in the paper. First, the recruitment description — a purchased MCH marketing list plus union and association distribution including social media, with no incentive, no reported response rate, and no weights — supports 'large and geographically diverse' but not the 'national sample' framing used throughout, and demographic comparability to NCES does not rule out selection on the constructs of interest. Second, the timing. The paper argues that measuring intentions at survey completion while asking retrospectively about 2019–20 for the mediators and victimization 'establish[es] causal order.' That claim appears in the Measures section without qualification and is retracted in the Limitations section ('methodologically cross-sectional, limiting our ability to determine the temporal order'). The administrator-support items, moreover, carry no time referent at all. On top of this, one of three items in each retention subscale explicitly names COVID-19, so the outcome is partly a measure of pandemic-specific displacement rather than general retention intent — which is a real constraint on transporting these estimates to a 2026 policy conversation about teacher shortages.

POLICY REACH VERSUS EVIDENTIARY REACH. Educational Researcher's audience makes the implications section consequential, and it travels well beyond the data. The recommendations — job-embedded professional development for administrators, an MTSS framework for staff supports, peer mentoring and coaching networks, coherent discipline policy — are plausible and grounded in the team's prior qualitative work, but nothing in this study measures professional development, discipline policy, or any intervention. The discipline argument leans on a single item ('My head of school or principal supports me in matters of discipline') buried in a three-item support scale, and then on citations to earlier papers. A reader should treat this section as expert opinion informed by a program of research, not as a policy conclusion licensed by these analyses.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE FIELD. Take this paper as solid correlational documentation that perceived administrator support is among the strongest teacher-reported correlates of intent to leave in a large national teacher sample, that the well-being pathways explain surprisingly little of that association, and that victimized teachers are worse off on every measure here. Take the moderation as a promising reframing with a statistically detectable but substantively small and imperfectly estimated effect. Do not take the title as a finding. The open question the paper most usefully poses — whether the value of a supportive principal genuinely diminishes for teachers under sustained student violence — remains open, and answering it will need longitudinal or administrative-data designs, non-pandemic samples, and independent measurement of administrator behavior.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

This AERA-flagship article carries no data availability statement, no code or Mplus syntax, no supplementary materials, and no stated pathway to the underlying APA Task Force survey data — and it also omits the sample-derivation, missing-data, and variable-construction details a replicator would need even with the data in hand. Against that, the reporting of the mediation model is unusually generous: Table 1's full correlation matrix lets a reader independently reproduce every coefficient in Table 2 to within rounding, which I verified. The paper's distinctive contribution — the victimization moderation in Table 3 and Figure 2 — is the part that is effectively unverifiable as printed.

**Strengths:**

- The analytic environment is named precisely: Mplus Version 8.8, MLR estimation, the MODEL INDIRECT command for indirect effects, and the DEFINE command for the product terms. Fit-index cutoffs (RMSEA < .05, CFI > .95, SRMR < .08) are pre-stated with a citation rather than chosen post hoc, and the McNeish et al. (2018) caveat about RMSEA is invoked in advance.
- Table 1 reports means, SDs, and the complete zero-order correlation matrix for all six study variables at N = 5,550. This is the single most valuable transparency feature in the paper: it makes the entire mediation model independently checkable without the raw data. Solving the normal equations from Table 1 alone (no covariates) returns support→transfer = -0.362 (reported -0.36), support→quit = -0.222 (-0.23), anxiety→quit = 0.244 (0.25), safety→quit = -0.115 (-0.11), anxiety→transfer = 0.152 (0.14), safety→transfer = -0.183 (-0.17), and all four indirect effects (-0.033, -0.055, -0.054, -0.035) match the reported -0.03, -0.05, -0.05, -0.03 exactly. Research Questions 1 and 2 are therefore fully verifiable from the published exhibits.
- Every coefficient in Tables 2 and 3 carries a standard error, an exact-or-bounded p value, and a 95% confidence interval — better uncertainty reporting than is typical in this literature.
- Full item wording is given for four of the five scales (administrator support, safety, anxiety/stress, transfer and quit), along with response anchors, reference periods, and internal-consistency coefficients (alpha for the continuous scales, KR-20 for the dichotomized victimization scale). Source instruments are cited (Griffith, 2004; Ting et al., 2002; McMahon, Worrell, et al., 2024).
- Reference categories are named explicitly for every categorical covariate (male, White/Caucasian, elementary school, suburban), so the covariate coding is unambiguous even though the covariate coefficients are never shown.
- The clustering decision is documented rather than asserted: a null model was run, state-level ICCs are reported with values (.006-.018), and the decision to forgo multilevel modeling follows from them. The limitations section further explains why school- and district-level clustering could not be assessed.
- Provenance is traceable. The parent survey is cited (McMahon et al., 2022, APA technical report), the recruitment vendor is named (MCH Strategic Data) with a description of how its database is built and maintained, IRB approval is attributed to a named institution, and funding, conflicts, and ORCIDs are all disclosed.

**Weaknesses:**

- No data availability statement, no open-practices statement, no supplementary materials, no appendix, no preregistration, and no repository link anywhere in the article. A keyword search of the full text for 'available', 'supplement', 'OSF', 'repository', 'syntax', 'deposit', 'appendix', and 'upon request' returns nothing relevant. The paper does not even offer the weak 'available upon request' formula, so there is no stated route — not one gated by a data-use agreement, not one gated by the APA Task Force — by which a reader could obtain these data.
- No Mplus input files, no MODEL statements, no MODEL CONSTRAINT or LOOP/PLOT code, no random seeds, and no analysis scripts. For a path model with three DEFINE-constructed product terms and a Johnson-Neyman-style plot, the syntax is the analysis, and none of it is shared.
- The analytic sample cannot be rebuilt. Recruitment was explicitly stratified by role across 'teachers, school psychologists, social workers, school staff, and administrators', but nothing states how the 5,550 teachers were extracted from that multi-role survey: whether role was self-identified, what the item looked like, whether pre-K and K-12 teachers were pooled by design, or what completion threshold qualified a case. There are no exclusion criteria of any kind, no count of invitations sent, no response rate, no cooperation rate, and no reconciliation of this N with the larger Ns reported in the sibling papers drawn from the same survey (McMahon, Worrell, et al., 2024; Reddy et al., 2024; Astor et al., 2024).
- Missing data are never addressed. The Participants section documents item-level missingness (110 no school level, 34 no gender, 69 no race/ethnicity, 24 no urbanicity), yet Tables 1, 2, and 3 all report N = 5,550. Under Mplus defaults, missingness on exogenous covariates produces listwise deletion unless the covariates' variances are brought into the model, which would drop the analytic N below 5,550. Whether FIML was used, whether covariates were modeled with distributional assumptions, or whether missing values were recoded to a category is nowhere stated — and neither is the missingness on age or on percent free/reduced-price lunch.
- Percentage of students receiving free/reduced-price lunch is used as a covariate in every equation but never described: no source (teacher self-report? a school identifier linked to CCD? an MCH database field?), no descriptive statistics, no missingness count, and no appearance in Table 1. A replicator cannot construct this variable at all.
- The key moderator is under-documented. The Educator Victimization Scale used '11 of the original 15 items' — the 11 are never listed and the 4 dropped are never named; only three example items appear. The rationale for dichotomizing 0-5 frequency responses to ever/never is not given, and whether the composite is a 0-11 count or a proportion is left to inference (M = 2.52, SD = 2.36 implies a count of dichotomized items). Composite construction is likewise unstated for the other scales, though their means on 1-5 anchors imply item averages, and whether the reverse-scored safety item was recoded before averaging is only implied.
- The Table 3 interaction model is not interpretable as printed and cannot be checked. Teacher victimization's 'standardized' main effects are -1.69 (on anxiety/stress) and -1.74 (on safety), with SEs of 0.05. A standardized coefficient of that magnitude is not a plausible effect size in a model whose outcomes are standardized, and the anxiety coefficient is the opposite sign from the zero-order correlation in Table 1 (r = +.36). The pattern is the signature of uncentered product terms — the 'main effect' becomes the conditional effect at administrator support = 0, which lies outside the 1-5 response range — compounded by Mplus's STDYX-type standardization being applied to a product variable, for which it is not a meaningful rescaling. Nothing in the text says whether the constituent variables were centered before DEFINE, or which standardization was requested.
- Figure 2's simple slopes cannot be regenerated from Table 3, and the two exhibits do not reconcile. In panel (a) the plotted conditional effect of support on anxiety/stress runs from about -0.20 at the low end of the moderator axis to about -0.128 at the high end, an implied interaction slope near 0.036 per moderator unit, against a tabled Support x Victimization coefficient of 0.40. The value at the axis midpoint (about -0.16) does not equal the tabled conditional effect (-0.19), and the same mismatch holds in panels (b), (c), and (d) (plotted midpoints of roughly 0.19, -0.31, and 0.36 against tabled 0.23, -0.26 for support→quit, and 0.25). Neither axis carries a variable name or units, the moderator axis runs -1.1 to 1.1 in an unstated metric, the two thin bounding lines are never identified as confidence bands, and no method for producing the plot is described.
- Figure 1 silently merges two different models. The paths labeled -.36, -.23, .28, -.19, -.17, -.11, .14, and .25 are the Table 2 (mediation) estimates, while -.42, .39, .12, and -.12 are Table 3 interaction coefficients drawn as if they were main-effect arrows from Teacher Victimization. Nothing in the figure or note distinguishes them. The .39 shown for Support x Victimization → anxiety does not match the 0.40 in Table 3. And although the note says only nonsignificant and covariate estimates are suppressed, the two largest and most significant coefficients in Table 3 (the -1.69 and -1.74 victimization main effects, both p < .001) do not appear in the figure.
- Model fit is reported without the ingredients needed to evaluate or reproduce it: no chi-square, no degrees of freedom, no count of free parameters, and no covariance-structure specification (are the anxiety and safety residuals correlated? the transfer and quit residuals? does anything predict administrator support?). Because the path estimates are recursive and reproduce from the correlation matrix without covariates, the reported misfit (RMSEA = .08, CFI = .91 for the mediation model) evidently arises from the covariate block rather than from the substantive structure — so the fit statistics are not diagnostic of the paths being interpreted. The mediation model's CFI of .91 also falls below the paper's own pre-stated >.95 threshold, and the text's justification requires 'values in acceptable ranges for all other indices', which is not satisfied here.
- Covariate coefficients are never reported, in any table or figure, for either model. The paper interprets a covariate-adjusted model whose adjustments are entirely invisible.
- Only standardized coefficients are reported. No unstandardized estimates, and no SDs for the product terms, appear anywhere — which is precisely what would be needed to recompute conditional effects, rebuild the simple slopes, or convert the moderation results to an interpretable metric.
- The measurement model is reported in a single line of global fit (RMSEA = .04, CFI = .95, SRMR = .04) with no factor loadings, no per-scale fit, no factor correlations, no chi-square, and no statement of how the 11 dichotomous victimization indicators were handled under MLR. It is also disconnected from the analysis: the CFA supports scales that are then collapsed into composites, so the measurement model constrains nothing in Tables 2 or 3.
- The sensitivity analysis in Note 1 — rerunning everything with victimization as a mean of the original 0-5 frequency scale rather than a count of dichotomized items — is reported only as 'results were unchanged and therefore not reported'. That substitution materially changes the moderator's scale and distribution, so it is the most informative robustness check in the paper, and it is the one a reader cannot see.
- The claim that 'demographics for the teacher sample in this study were comparable to national statistics' is asserted against two NCES sources with no comparison table and no statistics, so the representativeness argument for a nonprobability opt-in sample rests entirely on the reader's trust. No survey weights are used or discussed.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- You can verify the paper's mediation claims yourself, and should. Take the correlation matrix and Ns from Table 1, feed it to any SEM package as a covariance/correlation input (lavaan's sample.cov, Mplus TYPE=CORRELATION, or hand-solved normal equations), and estimate transfer and quit on support + anxiety + safety, with anxiety and safety each on support. Every coefficient in Table 2 reproduces within .015, and all four indirect effects reproduce exactly at the printed two decimals. Research Questions 1 and 2 do not require trusting the authors.
- That same reproduction tells you the covariate block is doing essentially nothing: the no-covariate estimates match the covariate-adjusted published ones to within rounding. Read the demographic and school controls as cosmetic rather than as adjustment that changes the answer, and do not credit the paper's framing of 'controlling for' these characteristics with much work.
- Do not use the Table 3 victimization main effects (-1.69, -1.74) as effect sizes, and do not cite them. They are almost certainly conditional effects at administrator support = 0 from uncentered product terms, standardized in a way that does not apply to products; the anxiety coefficient carries the opposite sign from the zero-order correlation in Table 1. Whatever they are, they are not the association between victimization and anxiety/safety.
- Treat the moderation findings — the paper's headline 'necessary but not sufficient' claim — as directionally suggestive but not quantitatively established. The four significant interactions cannot be recomputed from anything printed, Figure 2's plotted slopes are an order of magnitude smaller than Table 3's interaction coefficients, and Figure 2's midpoints do not equal Table 3's conditional effects. Before citing a magnitude, request the unstandardized estimates.
- If you contact the authors, ask for a specific short list rather than 'the materials': (a) the Mplus .inp files for both structural models and for whatever produced Figure 2; (b) unstandardized coefficients with SEs for both models, including the covariate block; (c) whether the DEFINE-constructed products used centered constituents and which STANDARDIZED output was reported; (d) the list of the 11 victimization items retained from the original 15; (e) the exact missing-data handling and the true analytic N per equation; (f) the source and coding of percent free/reduced-price lunch; and (g) the unreported Note 1 sensitivity results.
- Note the interaction-model fit paradox before treating the fit indices as validation. The moderation model reports better fit (RMSEA = .05, CFI = .93) than the simpler mediation model (RMSEA = .08, CFI = .91), and the mediation model's CFI falls below the paper's own stated .95 threshold. Since the substantive paths are recursive and just-identified given the mediators, the misfit is coming from the covariate block, not from the mediation structure — so these indices tell you nothing about whether the mediation story is right.
- When reading Figure 1, do not treat it as one model. Cross-check every coefficient against Tables 2 and 3 before quoting it: the arrows from Teacher Victimization are interaction terms from the Table 3 model, not main effects, and the remaining paths come from the Table 2 model. The .39 in the figure is 0.40 in Table 3.
- For the sample, go to the parent sources rather than this paper. McMahon, Worrell, et al. (2024, American Psychologist) and the McMahon et al. (2022) APA technical report describe the instrument and the recruitment design in more detail; use them to judge how the 5,550-teacher analytic sample relates to the full multi-role survey. This is an opt-in, vendor-list, non-probability sample from the 2020-21 pandemic year with no reported response rate and no weights, so generalization to 'U.S. teachers' is an assumption you are making, not a design property.
- Be alert to the overlapping-publication issue when you assess the weight of this evidence. At least four other papers analyze this same 2020-21 survey, and one of them (McMahon, Swenski, et al., 2024) tests a closely related model of teacher-directed violence, anxiety/stress, and transfer/quit intentions. Read the coefficients here as one specification from a shared dataset, not as independent corroboration of the sibling papers.
- If you intend to build on this, the reusable asset is Table 1, not Tables 2-3. The correlation matrix with N = 5,550 is enough to include this study in a meta-analytic SEM or to benchmark your own mediation estimates; the moderation results are not currently in a form anyone else can pool or extend.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Assessment is based on the complete article text plus direct inspection of Figures 1 and 2 rendered from the PDF at high resolution, and on an actual partial reproduction of Table 2 from Table 1.

The reproducibility picture here splits cleanly in two, and readers should hold the two halves to different standards of trust.

The mediation half is genuinely verifiable, and I verified it. Because the path model is recursive and estimated on composite scores, the full zero-order correlation matrix in Table 1 is sufficient to recover the structural coefficients. Solving the normal equations for the transfer and quit equations returns -0.362, 0.152, -0.183 and -0.222, 0.244, -0.115 against published values of -0.36, 0.14, -0.17 and -0.23, 0.25, -0.11; the four indirect effects come back as -0.033, -0.055, -0.054, -0.035 against published -0.03, -0.05, -0.05, -0.03. Two things follow. First, Research Questions 1 and 2 are independently checkable from the printed exhibits, which is more than most papers in this literature offer, and it partly compensates for the absent replication package. Second, since these are the no-covariate estimates and they land on the published covariate-adjusted values, the demographic and school controls are doing almost no work — which in turn means the reported model fit (RMSEA = .08, CFI = .91) reflects constraints in the covariate block rather than any test of the mediation structure. The substantive paths are effectively just-identified; their fit indices are decoration.

The moderation half — the paper's actual contribution and the source of its title — is not verifiable and does not internally cohere. Table 3 reports 'standardized' victimization main effects of -1.69 on anxiety/stress and -1.74 on safety, with SEs of 0.05 and CIs that exclude anything reasonable. The anxiety coefficient is opposite in sign to the +.36 zero-order correlation in Table 1. This is the classic uncentered-product signature: with administrator support measured on a 1-5 scale, the product term makes the victimization coefficient the conditional effect at support = 0, a value that does not exist in the data, and Mplus's STDYX standardization then divides a product variable by its own SD, which is not a meaningful rescaling for an interaction. The Methods section says only that the DEFINE command was used to generate the three product terms; centering is never mentioned, and which STANDARDIZED output was requested is never stated. As printed, these coefficients cannot be interpreted, converted, or checked.

Figure 2 compounds this rather than resolving it. It is not a conventional simple-slopes plot (outcome on y, predictor on x, separate lines at ±1 SD of the moderator) but a Johnson-Neyman-style plot of the conditional effect across moderator values with what appear to be confidence bands. Neither axis is labeled with a variable name or units; the moderator axis runs from about -1.1 to 1.1 in an unstated metric; the bounding lines are never identified. More seriously, it does not reconcile with Table 3. In panel (a) the conditional effect of support on anxiety/stress moves from roughly -0.20 to -0.128 across the full moderator range, an implied interaction slope near 0.036 per unit against a tabled coefficient of 0.40 — off by roughly an order of magnitude. The value at the axis midpoint (about -0.16) does not equal the tabled conditional effect (-0.19). The same failure to line up recurs in panels (b) through (d): plotted midpoints of about 0.19, -0.31, and 0.36 against tabled values of 0.23, -0.26, and 0.25. Whatever scaling Figure 2 is on, it is not the scaling of Table 3, and no reader can regenerate one from the other. Since no method for producing the figure is described and no code is shared, there is no way to adjudicate which exhibit is right.

Figure 1 has a distinct problem: it presents two different models as one diagram. Eight of the labeled paths are Table 2 (mediation) estimates; four (-.42, .39, .12, -.12) are Table 3 interaction coefficients drawn as arrows emanating from the Teacher Victimization ellipse, which visually represents interactions as main effects. Nothing in the note flags the mixture. The .39 disagrees with Table 3's 0.40. And although the note claims only nonsignificant and covariate estimates were suppressed, the two largest p < .001 coefficients in Table 3 — the -1.69 and -1.74 victimization main effects — are absent from the figure. Their omission is undisclosed.

On documentation of the data itself, the gaps are broad rather than deep in any one place, but they accumulate past the point where a replication could proceed even with the raw file. A keyword sweep of the full text confirms there is no data availability statement, no open-practices badge, no supplementary material, no appendix, no repository, no preregistration, and not even an 'available upon request' clause. Recruitment was stratified across five roles, yet how the 5,550 teachers were separated from school psychologists, social workers, staff, and administrators is never described — not the role item, not whether pre-K was pooled with K-12 by design, not any completion threshold. There is no invitation count and no response rate, which for a vendor-list opt-in survey is the number that determines how much the 'national sample' framing is worth. Item-level missingness is documented in the Participants section (110, 34, 69, and 24 cases across school level, gender, race/ethnicity, and urbanicity) and then contradicted by an unchanging N = 5,550 in all three tables, with no statement of FIML, listwise deletion, or covariate modeling; under Mplus defaults with exogenous covariates, the analytic N should have fallen. Percent free/reduced-price lunch enters every equation with no source, no descriptives, and no missingness count. The moderator scale lists 3 of its 11 items and never says which 4 of the original 15 were dropped. Composite construction (mean versus sum, and handling of the reverse-scored safety item) is inferable from the reported means but never stated. And the measurement model is a single line of global fit with no loadings, no per-scale fit, and no account of how 11 dichotomous indicators were estimated under MLR — a model that, since the analysis uses composites, constrains nothing downstream anyway.

One more item deserves flagging because it is the most informative unreported result in the paper. Note 1 states that all primary analyses were rerun with victimization scored as the mean of the original 0-5 frequency scale rather than as a count of dichotomized items, and that 'results were unchanged and therefore not reported.' That substitution changes the moderator's metric, variance, and distributional shape substantially, and it is exactly the check a skeptical reader would want given the dichotomization decision is itself unjustified. Reporting it as a one-line assurance places the paper's most load-bearing robustness evidence entirely outside verification.

On calibration: 'weak' rather than 'insufficient' because Research Questions 1 and 2 really are reproducible from what is printed, the estimator and software are specified precisely, uncertainty is reported throughout, and the clustering decision is documented with actual ICC values. 'Weak' rather than 'adequate' because for a 2026 article in AERA's flagship journal there is no data statement of any kind, no code for a model whose central results depend on hand-constructed product terms, no sample-derivation or missing-data documentation, and headline moderation results that are simultaneously uninterpretable in the table and unreconcilable with the figure meant to illustrate them.
